 TENDON - task description
 TENDON is used for the calculation of prestressing loads for beam, slabs and shell structures. Essential components of the module are the generation of duct and tendon geometries, the intersection of the ducts with the static system as well as the simulation of the prestressing process and the friction losses.
 The forces of the prestressing are stored as loads on the intersected beam and quad elements in the database.
 Elastic shortening is not considered in TENDON, but can be determined with the corresponding structural analysis modules of SOFiSTiK, especially ASE.
 Important
 The dimensioning of the prestressing is critical for the stability of a prestressed struc- ture. The user of TENDON should therefore convince himself about the accuracy and sensitivity of the prestressing parameters including their effects. A check of the results by means of rough engineering estimates is indispensable.
 1.1 Process in TENDON
 The classical calculation process of TENDON is as follows:
 1. Definition of the prestressing systems (SYSP).
 2. Determination of the reference axes (AXES).
 oa WD
 3. Determination of the duct geometries (TGEO).
 4. Determination of the prestressing sequence (PSIG, PAAS, PFAC or PDEF).
 5. Determination of the tendons and prestressing forces (TEND).
 6. Tabular and graphical output of the reference axes, duct geometries, tendons and pre- stressing forces (ECHO and PLOT).
 In the case of the calculation of flat slabs, there is an alternative input (SLAB), where reference axes, duct geometries and tendons are generated simultaneously.
 1.2 Embedding in the SOFiSTiK process
 In the classical and the graphical environment of SOFiSTiK, it is possible to prestress differ- ent structures with TENDON, e.g., shell structures, beams, flat slabs and bridge structures in CABD (Computer-Aided Bridge Design). Only the prestressing of volume structures is currently not supported.

In the classical and the graphical environment of SOFiSTiK, it is possible to prestress differ- ent structures with TENDON, e.g., shell structures, beams, flat slabs and bridge structures in CABD (Computer-Aided Bridge Design). Only the prestressing of volume structures is currently not supported..
 In the simulation process, TENDON is typically executed after the system generation.
 An exemplary workflow in the CABD environment could look as follows:
 1. Definition of a parametric master cross-section.
 2. Modelling of the global system axis with placements and variables.
 3. Modelling of secondary- and sub-structures.
 oa
 4. Generation of the static system (meshing).
 5. Definition of the prestressing system (TENDON).
 6. Determination of the prestressing geometries along the system axis and evaluation of prestressing loads (TENDON).
 7. Definition of further loads.
 8. Definition of the construction stages.
 9. Calculation and design.
 2 Theoretical principles

Tendons and ducts are usually modelled in an unrolled form along a reference axis. The definition of the tendon is hierarchically based on the following data structures:
 Reference axis The reference axis is the basic geometry on which the constraining points of the duct geometry are defined. The reference axis can be taken from another programme (e.g. SOFiMSHC, SOFiPLUS) or can be created in TENDON. Several ducts can refer to the same reference axis.
 Duct The duct geometry is usually defined relative to the reference axis with u- and v-values, but can also be generated with an existing curve. A duct can contain several tendons.
 Tendon Tendon geometries are defined on duct geometries. The difference between tendon and duct geometry is that (i) the tendon can be defined only on a section of the duct and (ii) it can have an eccentricity with respect to the duct geometry.

The image is a three‐dimensional, perspective view of a single prestressed concrete beam segment, shown in light and darker shades of gray to distinguish its major geometric features. The beam comprises a broad, flat top flange (rendered in light gray) and a narrower, deeper web region supporting two smaller, T‐shaped ribs (shown in darker gray) below it. The overall shape resembles an inverted I‐ or T‐beam with additional stiffening ribs.  

At the front edge of the beam’s top flange, a local coordinate system is illustrated by three colored arrows, each originating from the same point on the beam’s front‐facing corner (this point corresponds to “S,” the local origin on the reference axis described in the accompanying text). The red arrow, labeled “x,” extends diagonally upward and into the depth of the top flange, indicating the local x‐direction (tangential to the reference axis). The green arrow, labeled “y,” runs horizontally along the flange, pointing to the right; this marks the local y‐axis, orthogonal to x and lying in the plane of the flange. The blue arrow, labeled “z,” projects straight downward from the same origin, perpendicular to the flange; this defines the local z‐axis, typically aligned with gravity.  

Below the beam graphic, the caption “Figure 2.1: Coordinate systems.” appears, tying the visual back to the surrounding discussion on global, local, and element coordinate frames. Although only one coordinate frame is depicted, it clearly demonstrates how a local system is affixed at a point on the structural element, with the x‐axis in the tangential direction of the reference axis, the y‐axis orthogonal and lying in the cross‐section plane, and the z‐axis normal to that plane—often coinciding with the direction of gravity.  

Subtle shading on the beam’s faces helps convey its three‐dimensional form: the top flange is uniformly light, the web beneath it is slightly darker, and the inner T‐shaped stiffeners are darkest. All edges are drawn with thin black outlines. Together, the geometry and axis arrows articulate the notion of a local coordinate system that follows a curved or straight reference axis used in tendon modeling and prestressing analysis.

When describing tendons, three different coordinate systems can be distinguished (see Figure 2.1):
 Global coordinate system The orientation of the global coordinate system is defined during system generation (e.g. in SOFiMSHC or SOFiPLUS). It must be described as a Cartesian coordinate system with the Z-axis usually pointing in the di- rection of gravity (downwards).
 Local coordinate system For curved reference axes, the local coordinate system can vary along the curve. The origin is at the corresponding point S on the reference axis and the local x-direction points in the tangential direction. The local y- and z- axes are orthogonal and are defined differently depending on how the reference axis was created:
 • Beam sequence: For the case that the reference axis was created with beams, the reference axis is orthogonal to the beam cross-sections and the local y- and z-directions are defined according to the cross-sectional coordinate system.
 •
 3D curve: If the reference axis was defined with a 3D curve, the y- and z-axis are referred to the global coordinates. Usually the local z-axis lies on the plane spanned by the local x-axis and the global Z-axis.
 Local coordinates U or V always refer to the local y- or z-axis of the coordi- nate system of the reference axis.
 Element coordinate system The prestressing loads are stored in the respective coordinate system of the elements. In the case of beams, this is the cross-sectional coordinate system, which is normally identical to the local coordinate system
 of the reference axis.

The image is a schematic, side-view cross-section of a prestressing duct with its internal tendon path offset from the duct’s geometric centerline, illustrating the concept of maximum eccentricity (εₘ or εₘₐₓ). The duct is represented by a long, horizontally oriented rectangle shaded light gray, with solid dark-gray borders defining its top and bottom walls. Within this rectangular envelope, two centerlines are drawn:

1. A dashed gray line running centrally through the duct’s interior, tracing the nominal or designed geometry of the duct itself as it gently undulates up and down.  
2. A solid blue line, identical in overall curvature to the dashed line but shifted upward toward the upper duct wall wherever the duct curves. This blue line represents the actual path of the tendon bundle, which does not completely fill the duct and therefore, under gravity or bending, leans against one side of the duct wall in regions of curvature.

At three distinct points along the duct’s curved profile—near the first crest, the central trough, and the second crest—double-headed arrows are drawn between the dashed and blue lines. Each arrow is annotated “εₘₐₓ,” signifying the maximum radial deviation (eccentricity) between the designed duct axis and the actual tendon centroid. These arrows are perpendicular to the dashed centerline, visually conveying the distance by which the tendon’s center of gravity shifts toward the wall at the points of greatest curvature.

Beneath the diagram, a caption reads:
“Figure 2.2: Maximum eccentricity εₘₐₓ.”

Taken together, the drawing conveys the following key points in the context of prestressed concrete design and tendon layout:

• Duct Geometry Drives Tendon Path: The shape of the internal duct—defined by design approvals and axis restrictions—dictates the nominal tendon geometry, shown by the dashed line.  
• Eccentricity Definition: Because the tendon bundle does not exactly conform to the duct’s mid-axis, its centroid will lean against one side in curved segments, producing an offset defined as the eccentricity ε, measured as the radial distance from the duct axis to the tendon CG.  
• Maximum Eccentricity Control: Users can specify a maximum allowable eccentricity εₘ in the prestressing system parameters (e.g., SYSP ECC). If no limit is set, the tendon is assumed to fully follow the duct geometry, i.e., εₘ = 0 so the tendon remains centered along the duct axis.  
• Visual Verification: The graphical representation allows engineers to verify compliance with edge and axis restrictions and ensure that the specified maximum eccentricity is not exceeded anywhere along the tendon profile.

The geometry of the tendons is defined by the duct geometry. The user must ensure that all edge and axis restrictions of the duct are maintained according to the respective approval. The shape of the evaluated geometries can be checked with the help of the graphical representa- tion.
 Since a tendon does not completely fill the inside of a duct, the tendon will lean against one side of the wall in areas of curvature. The maximum deviation from the duct axis to the centre of gravity of the wire bundle is called eccentricity (see figure 2.2). The user can specify the maximum eccentricity ϵm in the prestressing system (SYSP ECC). If no eccentricity is specified, the tendon geometry corresponds to the duct geometry (on the corresponding section).

The image is a clean, two-column–style excerpt from a technical manual on post-tensioning tendon friction losses. It begins with a one-line introduction in a standard serif font:

“For post-tensioning tendons, the losses of stressing force due to frictions are calculated as follows:”

Below that line, two numbered equations appear side by side (or one immediately following the other), each set in display format with a slightly larger math font. They read:

  (2.1) P(x) = P₀ · e^(–μ [A(x) + β·x])  (Stressing)  
  (2.2) P′(x) = P₀′ · e^(–μ [A(0) + β·x])  (Slip)

Here:
 • P₀ is labeled “Jacking force.”  
 • P₀′ is “Jacking force after slip.”  
 • μ is defined as “Friction coefficient between tendon and duct.”  
 • s (represented implicitly via the function argument x) is “Arc length from the jacking location.”  
 • A(x) is the “Sum of intentional angular displacements along the tendon until x.”  
 • β is the “Wobble factor,” i.e. the unintentional angular displacements per unit length due to imperfections.

Immediately beneath these equations there is a short “Remark” in smaller italic text:
“In some standards (e.g. AASHTO or IRC), the corresponding factor k contains already the friction coefficient μ. This must be taken into account when defining β (see explanation on BETA in the SYSP record).”

Following the remark, another centered, numbered formula (2.3) is shown:

  k = β · μ ⇒ β = k / μ

Underneath, two brief unnumbered paragraphs appear in normal font:

  • “An example of the calculation of the jacking force loss can be found in chapter 4.”  
  • “For the specification of additional friction losses via the record FRIC. These are considered as angular displacements per length (similar to β).”

Finally, the excerpt closes with a note on force-loss behavior:

  “Figure 2. Qualitative tension force curve due to friction losses. The system is symmetrical on both sides, with additional releasing and re-tensioning on both sides.”

Visually, the layout alternates between plain text blocks, display-style equations flush-centered with equation numbers in parentheses at right, and succinct definitions formatted as bullet or lead-in lines. The fonts remain consistent: Times/serif for body text and slightly larger math font for equations, with italic styling reserved for the single “Remark” sentence.

The illustration is a schematic force-versus-length diagram (Figure 2.3) showing how post-tensioning tendon forces evolve along the length of a tendon that is stressed from both ends, taking into account friction losses and multiple stressing cycles. Although the horizontal axis is unlabeled, it represents the arc length x measured from some origin (often the jacking location), and the vertical axis represents the instantaneous tendon force P(x).  

Key graphical elements:  
• Two opposing friction-decay curves (shown as gently sloping dotted lines) emanate from each end of the tendon. On the right these curves are labeled (1) and (3), and on the left they’re labeled (5) and (7). Each dotted curve represents the theoretical force profile along the tendon if you “stressed” from one end only, losing force exponentially or according to P(x)=Pₚ·e^{–μ·(A(x)+β·x)}.  
• A horizontal dashed line across the middle marks the jack’s peak force (the ideal no-loss target).  
• Superimposed on the dotted decay curves is a sawtooth-shaped solid red line. This shows the actual force profile after successive operations: stressing, releasing, re-stressing and finally slipping back each end.  
• Vertical blue lines indicate the specific points along the tendon where load cycles occur. There are four blue lines near each end (eight total): these mark the positions of the jacks or anchorage points when force is applied or released.  

Legend (to the right of the plot) clarifies the numbering:  
  – Right-hand end:  
     1. stressing  
     2. releasing  
     3. re-stressing  
     4. slip  
  – Left-hand end:  
     5. stressing  
     6. releasing  
     7. re-stressing  
     8. slip  

Interpretation of the red sawtooth:  
1. Starting at the right end, the tendon is stressed to the target (point 1 on the upper right), reaching nearly the dashed jacking-force line.  
2. After release (2), the actual force drops slightly (point 2 lies on the friction-decay dotted curve).  
3. A re-stress cycle (3) again raises the force but not quite to the original peak—friction has eaten away some capacity—so the red line peaks lower than the dashed line.  
4. Finally, the tendon “slips” to seating (4), and the force relaxes along the friction curve from that jacking point.  

The same sequence then repeats from the left end (points 5–8), but because friction losses accumulate in opposite directions, the profiles mirror one another: the left-originating dotted curves slope upward toward the center, while the right-originating ones slope downward. In the central zone the two red segments join, showing the net force balance where the stress fronts meet.  

Overall, this graphic conveys how each stressing cycle and each frictional loss incrementally reduces the achievable tendon force as you move away from the jacking end, and why multiple stressing (“touch-up”) cycles and careful accounting for curvature (A(x)) and wobble (β·x) are needed to approach the desired prestress level at mid-span.

The table shown defines five discrete “records” that can appear in an input deck, together with the list of data “items” each record accepts. In the context of SOFiSTiK’s input-file syntax (and in line with the general manual “Basics,” which already covers the HEAD, END, UNIT, SIZE and PAGE records), this fragment spells out the optional parameters you can specify to control debugging output, file echoing, time delays, exposition levels and geometric export. Below is a structured walk-through of each record and its constituent items:

1. CTRL (Control record)  
   • OPT (optional flag)  
   • VAL (value)  
   – Purpose: The CTRL record is used to switch on or off certain predefined control features at run-time. “OPT” designates which control channel (for example, error checking, memory diagnostics, verbosity), while “VAL” sets the numerical or logical level (e.g. 0 = off, 1 = on, higher integers for gradated detail).  

2. ECHO (Echo record)  
   • OPT (optional flag)  
   • VAL (value)  
   – Purpose: ECHO determines whether the input deck should be “echoed” back into the listing or log file. “OPT” specifies which sections to echo (e.g. geometry, load definitions, results processing), and “VAL” toggles the echo ON/OFF or selects the verbosity of the echo stream.  

3. TDEL (Time-delay record)  
   • TYPE (delay type)  
   • NO (identifier)  
   – Purpose: TDEL is used to introduce programmatic pauses or synchronization delays—for instance, when multiple parallel processes must be staged. “TYPE” names the delay category (e.g. CPU wait, I/O sync) and “NO” is a unique index so that multiple TDEL records can be distinguished and referenced elsewhere.  

4. EXPO (Exposition record)  
   • OPT (optional flag)  
   • TO (destination)  
   – Purpose: The EXPO record controls the level or destination of additional exposition or diagnostic commentary during execution. “OPT” selects which information to expose (e.g. internal data structures, performance metrics), and “TO” may specify an output channel (command window, file, console).  

5. GEOX (Geometry-export record)  
   • NOG (number of geometries)  
   • TYPG (geometry type code)  
   • FROM (start index)  
   • TO (end index)  
   • INC (increment step)  
   • OUTP (output format)  
   • CSP (coordinate system parameter)  
   – Purpose: GEOX is the most elaborate of the five. It defines how and which portions of the model geometry are written out to external files or subroutines. “NOG” gives the count of distinct geometric entities; “TYPG” classifies them (e.g. points, lines, shells); “FROM/TO/INC” let you extract a subset by index range; “OUTP” chooses between text vs. binary, or neutral vs. native CAD formats; “CSP” may designate the coordinate system or transformation to apply on export.  

Sequence and Context Notes  
– The order in which these records appear in your input deck follows the recommended workflow: set run-time controls (CTRL), decide on echo behavior (ECHO), introduce any needed delays (TDEL), activate additional reporting (EXPO), and finally export geometry (GEOX).  
– Upstream of these five, the foundational records HEAD, END, UNIT, SIZE, PAGE (and any others you may require) are described in the SOFiSTiK: Basics manual and should bracket or precede this block.

The input table defines the syntax and semantics of two fields—OPT and VAL—used to configure global control parameters for the TENDON module (see also TGEO, TEND).  This table would be parsed into a RAG vector store so that downstream components (for example, query engines or auto-completion agents) can recognize and validate CTRL records that adjust intersection tolerances.

1. Table Layout  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword or field name in the CTRL record  
     – Description: a human-readable explanation of that keyword or field  
     – Unit: the expected data type or measurement unit  
     – Default: the default value assumed if none is supplied  
   • Rows  
     – OPT: selects which control parameter is being modified  
     – VAL: supplies the numeric (or literal) value corresponding to OPT  

2. Detailed Field Definitions  
   a) OPT (Unit = LIT4, Default = “–”)  
      • Type: a 4-character literal (LIT4)  
      • Purpose: specifies which of three tolerance parameters will be set or overridden in the TENDON module’s global control record.  Only one of the following may appear per CTRL OPT statement:  
        1. OFFN  
           • “Limit distance for intersections in normal direction”  
           • Governs how far an intersection of a duct (TGEO) or tendon (TEND) may lie outside a finite-element element in its local normal direction and still be treated as “internal.”  The default OFFN is 0.5 m.  
        2. OFFI  
           • “Limit distance for intersections in plane direction”  
           • Controls the maximum allowable gap (in the plane of quad elements) through which a tendon may pass without explicit mesh intersection.  The default OFFI is 0.02 m.  
        3. SNAP  
           • “Tolerance for the snapping of beam intersections”  
           • Defines how close (along the beam axis) an intersection must be to a beam’s end-points before being automatically snapped to that end.  The default SNAP is 0.001 m.  
      • Default: none.  OPT must be provided to indicate which parameter is to be set.

   b) VAL (Unit = “–”, Default = “*”)  
      • Type: a numeric value (floating point), in meters, matching the OPT parameter’s unit.  
      • Purpose: provides the new setting for the chosen tolerance.  For example, if OPT=OFFN and VAL=0.7, the normal-direction intersection tolerance becomes 0.7 m.  
      • Default “*”: indicates that if no explicit value is given, the system’s built-in default (OFFN=0.5 m, OFFI=0.02 m, SNAP=0.001 m) remains in force.

3. Usage Illustration  
   • CTRL OPT OFFN VAL 0.7[m]  
     – Raises the allowable normal-direction intersection offset from 0.5 m to 0.7 m.  
   • CTRL OPT OFFI VAL 0.1[m]  
     – Widens the planar gap threshold from 0.02 m to 0.1 m, capturing potential through-mesh tendon passages.  
   • CTRL OPT SNAP VAL 0.1[m]  
     – Extends the beam end snap tolerance from 1 mm to 100 mm, so intersections falling within 0.1 m of a beam endpoint will be snapped.

4. Contextual Notes  
   – For quad meshes, even external intersections can be recorded and later corrected via ASE loads (see ASE CTRL QTYP V2 1).  
   – In curved or composite meshes, insufficient OFFI may lead to missed intersections; raising OFFI flags them as internal.  
   – Box girders are treated as internal intersections regardless of tendon path.

By feeding this table into a RAG vector store, any component needing to interpret or suggest CTRL records for tendon-mesh intersection tolerances can quickly retrieve the syntax, valid options, expected units, and system defaults.

The table defines the two parameters (“items”) that drive the behavior of the ECHO command, which in turn controls which data are written into a report and how much detail appears.  Both parameters share the same data type (a four-character literal, or LIT4) but have different roles and defaults.  In essence, you invoke ECHO by specifying an OPT (what to print) and a VAL (how much to print).

1.  OPT (“Option”)
    •  Type: LIT4  
    •  Default: FULL  
    •  Role: Selects one or more categories of data to include in the report.  You can specify a single literal from the list below or simply use FULL to turn on every category at once.  
    •  Available literals:
       – SYSP   : Prestressing system  
       – AXES   : Reference axis definitions  
       – TOPP   : Span definitions (TOPology of Prestressing Profile)  
       – TGEO   : Duct geometry  
       – TEND   : Tendon overview (summary per tendon)  
       – GEOM   : Tendon geometry (full line-by-line description)  
       – LOAD   : Tendon loads and friction forces  
       – SLAB   : Slabs; if set to FULL, slab data are exported to a .dat file  
       – MASS   : Overview of steel masses (per tendon, etc.)  
       – COND   : Overview of all tendons (summary across entire model)  
       – PLOT   : Activation or de-activation of plots (on-screen or file output)  
       – FULL   : All of the above categories  

2.  VAL (“Value”)
    •  Type: LIT4  
    •  Default: YES  
    •  Role: Defines the verbosity or extent of the output for the categories selected by OPT.  
    •  Available literals:
       – NO     : Do not produce output for the given OPT category  
       – YES    : Produce regular (standard) output  
       – FULL   : Produce extensive output (where supported by the category)  

How to interpret the table in context:  
– If you issue “ECHO FULL YES” (the shorthand for setting OPT=FULL, VAL=YES), you request that every possible data category be written into the report at its standard level of detail.  
– If you later issue “ECHO TGEO FULL”, you are refining the TGEO category so that duct geometry is reported in full, overriding its default regular granularity.  
– Conversely, “ECHO MASS NO” would suppress the steel-mass overview entirely, even though the default for VAL is YES.  

Taken together, these two parameters let you tailor the ECHO command very precisely.  You choose which data streams (OPT) you want, and then you choose how much detail to expose (VAL).  Defaults (OPT=FULL, VAL=YES) guarantee that, unless overridden, you get a standard report covering all prestressing data.  For finer control—say, omitting certain tables, or demanding exhaustive geometry details—you mix and match the literals in successive ECHO statements.

See also: SYSP, AXES, TOPP, TGEO, TEND, GEOX, SLAB

Below is a comprehensive description of the three input items defined for the TDEL command. This information is intended to support indexing and retrieval in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, and to guide users in selectively deleting prestressing data.

1. Overview of TDEL  
   • Purpose: Remove prestressing information from the database, including tendons and any loadings that were generated by the TENDON routine.  
   • Scope:  
     – If an item’s value is set to 0, it acts as a wildcard and all records of that type are deleted.  
     – Loadings created by other modules (e.g. AQB TEND) remain untouched.  
   • Recommendation: Place the TDEL command inside its own PROG TENDON block. This ensures that it executes only after all tendon-related input has been read, preventing partial or incorrect deletions.

2. Input Items and Their Attributes  
   The table below lists each keyword, its meaning, units (if any), and its default value.

   • AXES  
     – Description: Identifier of the reference axis (or axis system) whose entire hierarchy of children and associated prestressing data you wish to delete.  
     – Unit: None (dimensionless integer).  
     – Default: 0 (deletes all axes and all tendons under every axis).  

   • TGEO  
     – Description: Identifier of the duct geometry. Ducts represent the physical path or conduit in which a tendon is placed. Selecting a non-zero TGEO deletes only the prestressing elements associated with that geometry.  
     – Unit: None (dimensionless integer).  
     – Default: 0 (deletes all duct geometries).  

   • TEND  
     – Description: Identifier of a specific tendon. This enables the most granular level of deletion, removing exactly the named tendon (and its TENDON-generated loadings).  
     – Unit: None (dimensionless integer).  
     – Default: 0 (deletes all tendons).  

3. Combination Logic  
   – You can specify one, two or all three keywords in a single TDEL statement.  
   – Any item omitted or explicitly set to zero acts as “delete all” in its category.  
   – Examples:  
     • “TDEL 0”  
       · Equivalent to “TDEL AXES 0 TGEO 0 TEND 0”  
       · Deletes every axis, every duct geometry and every tendon—along with all TENDON-generated loadings.  
     • “TDEL AXES 100 TEND 0”  
       · Deletes axis #100 and its entire subtree of axes.  
       · Deletes every tendon within those axes.  
       · Deletes all loadings created by TENDON for those tendons.  
       · Does not touch tendons or loadings outside axis #100, nor loadings created by other modules.  
     • “TDEL TGEO 25 TEND 7”  
       · Deletes only tendon #7 in geometry #25.  
       · Leaves all other ducts, axes and tendons intact.

4. Best Practices  
   • Always wrap TDEL in a dedicated PROG TENDON block to ensure that all relevant tendon definitions have been processed before deletion.  
   • Use zero values sparingly; unintentional “delete all” actions can remove large swaths of data.  
   • Cross-reference with AXES, TGEO and TEND input records to plan selective cleanup—especially in large models with hundreds of prestressing elements.

The table you’re looking at summarizes the various ways in which the TDEL command can selectively delete prestressing (tendon) information from the database. In other words, it shows all combinations of the three primary identifiers—AXES, TGEO and TEND—that you can pass to TDEL, together with a plain-English “erase action” description and an outline of what else gets removed (“Affects also”) whenever that combination is used.

Table structure  
• Columns  
  1. AXES: Reference axis number or keyword (or 0 for “all axes”)  
  2. TGEO: Duct geometry number or keyword (or blank if not specified)  
  3. TEND: Tendon identifier or keyword (or blank if not specified)  
  4. Erase action: Natural-language summary of exactly what is being deleted.  
  5. Affects also: What additional data (TGEO, TEND or loadings) is cascaded and removed as a side effect.  

• Special rules  
  – An input value of 0 in any of the first three fields means “delete every element of that type.”  
  – Any field left blank (“–”) is simply not part of the selection criteria.  
  – Loadings generated by TENDON (the tendon-processing module) are always considered; loadings created by other means (e.g. AQB TEND) are not removed.  
  – Best practice: Place TDEL in its own PROG TENDON block so that deletions happen only after all tendon input records have been read—this prevents partial or incorrect purging.  

Row-by-row interpretation  
1. AXES=0, TGEO=–, TEND=–  
   • Erase action: “All reference axes.”  
   • Affects also: All TGEO entries, all TEND entries and all loadings.  
   • In plain terms: TDEL 0 wipes out every axis definition in the model. Because every duct geometry and tendon is linked to at least one axis, they also get deleted, as do all tendon loadings.  

2. AXES=NOH, TGEO=–, TEND=–  
   • Erase action: “Reference axis NOH.”  
   • Affects also: Any TGEO entries, tendons and loadings that are children (directly or indirectly) of axis NOH.  
   • In practice: TDEL AXES NOH removes just the one axis named NOH plus any geometries or tendons that were built on it, and their associated loadings. Elements tied to other axes remain untouched.  

3. AXES=–, TGEO=NOG, TEND=–  
   • Erase action: “Duct geometry NOG.”  
   • Affects also: All tendons and loadings that use duct geometry NOG.  
   • In practice: TDEL TGEO NOG deletes that specific duct layout from the database and all prestressing elements defined on it. Other geometries and their tendons survive.  

4. AXES=–, TGEO=–, TEND=NOT  
   • Erase action: “Tendon NOT.”  
   • Affects also: All loadings that have been generated by TENDON for tendon NOT.  
   • In practice: TDEL TEND NOT purges only the single named tendon and its auto-generated loading records. It leaves other tendons, geometries and axes in place.  

Examples from the documentation  
• “$ Delete everything”  
 TDEL 0  
• “$ Delete reference axis 100 with all children and all tendons (and loadings)”  
 TDEL AXES 100 TEND 0

The table defines the available fields (records) of the GEOX command, which you use to export the three-dimensional or station-based geometry of ducts (TYPG = DUCT) or tendons (TYPG = TEND) into text, CSV, database or report output.  Each row describes one parameter (“Item”), its meaning, the unit or literal type, and its default value or requirement.  

1. NOG  
• Description: Identifier of the geometry to export. Depending on TYPG, this is either the duct geometry ID (TGEO) or the tendon ID (TEND).  
• Unit/Type: none (—)  
• Default: mandatory (!)  

2. FROM / TO  
• Description: Defines the segment of the curve to output. FROM is the start station, TO the end station along the reference axis. If omitted, the entire curve is exported.  
• Unit/Type: none (—)  
• Defaults: both are optional (*), but use them together if you need a subsection.  

3. INC  
• Description: Controls point sampling along the curve. If INC > 0, it is the distance (in metres) between consecutive output points. If INC < 0, its absolute value is the total number of output points to generate between FROM and TO.  
• Unit: none (—)  
• Default: 0.5  

4. TYPG  
• Description: Selects whether you export a duct (DUCT) or a tendon (TEND).  
• Type: literal, 4 chars (LIT4)  
• Default: DUCT  

5. OUTP  
• Description: Specifies which coordinates or properties to include in the export. You may combine any of the literals S, U, V, X, Y, Z:  
  – S: station along reference axis  
  – U: lateral offset in local y-direction  
  – V: vertical offset in local z-direction  
  – X,Y,Z: three-dimensional coordinates in global system  
• Type: literal (LIT)  
• Default: S U V X Y Z  

6. CSP  
• Description: If you want U and V offsets measured relative to a cross-section point (CSP) rather than the reference axis, supply the CSP identifier here. If the CSP (or beam) is missing at a station, U/V revert to the reference axis.  
• Type: literal, 4 chars (LIT4)  
• Default: none (–)  

7. DU / DV  
• Description: Nominal offset applied to the U (local y) and V (local z) coordinates before computing superelevation.  
• Unit: metres [m] (database code 1001)  
• Default: 0.0  

8. FACH  
• Description: Superelevation factor. Only affects U and V via: Une = (Uod + DU) · FACH.  
• Unit/Type: none (—)  
• Default: 1.0  

9. EXPO  
• Description: Destination of the output. Choose one of:  
  – TXT: write a .uv text file  
  – CSV: write a .csv file  
  – GAX: export into the geometry-axis database  
  – PLB: include in the report  
• Type: literal, 4 chars  
• Default: PLB  

10. AXID  
• Description: When exporting to the database (EXPO = GAX), AXID sets the identifier of the newly created axis record.  
• Type: LIT4  
• Default: mandatory when EXPO = GAX (*), otherwise optional  

11. TITL  
• Description: Optional title of the output file or report section.  
• Type: literal, up to 32 chars (LIT32)  
• Default: none (–)  

12. SEP  
• Description: Decimal separator to use in TXT or CSV files:  
  – COMA: decimal comma (1,00m)  
  – DOT: decimal point (1.00m)  
• Type: literal, 4 chars  
• Default: COMA

The table defines the structure of the SYSP (prestressing system) record – and its simplified cousin SYSS (pre-tensioning system) – in a tendon‐analysis input deck. Each row corresponds to one keyword (“Item”) that must be supplied when you define a prestressing system. The four columns are:

 • Item  
   – The exact name of the parameter as it must appear in the input file (e.g. “ZV,” “BETA,” “SP”).  
 • Description  
   – A concise English explanation of what the parameter means or controls.  
 • Unit  
   – The physical unit expected in the input. Units flagged with an underscore and bracket (e.g. [kN]₁₀₂₈) indicate that the number must carry that unit, or a compatible one if explicitly annotated.  
 • Default  
   – The value assumed if you omit this item. An exclamation mark (!) means “no default allowed – you must specify it.” If the cell contains another item name, that item’s value will be used by default (e.g. LFIX defaults to LPRE).

Below is a grouped overview of all parameters:

1. Identification  
   • NOPS (–, mandatory)  
     → Unique ID of the prestressing system.  
   • MAT (–, mandatory)  
     → Material number referring to the prestressing steel grade.  
   • TITL (LIT32, default “–”)  
     → Free‐text title of the system.

2. Force reference  
   • ZV ([kN], mandatory)  
     → Reference force for limit checks (PFAC) and reporting. Usually set to the anchor‐set force Pm0 but otherwise arbitrary.

3. Tendon geometry & configuration  
   • AZ ([mm²], mandatory)  
     → Total steel cross‐sectional area of the tendon (all strands or wires).  
   • LITZ (–, default 1)  
     → Number of wires or strands in the tendon bundle.  
   • MINR ([m], mandatory)  
     → Minimum allowable curvature radius of the tendon path.  
   • DO ([mm], mandatory)  
     → Outer diameter of the duct enclosing the tendon.

4. Friction & wobble losses  
   • BETA ([deg/m], mandatory)  
     → Wobble (geometry-induced) friction coefficient. Default unit is degrees per meter; other units (e.g. 1/m) are accepted if annotated.  
   • BETG ([deg/m], default = BETA)  
     → Wobble coefficient for straight (PTSV) geometries; defaults to BETA.  
   • MUE (–, mandatory)  
     → Friction coefficient during stressing.  
   • MUE- (–, default = MUE)  
     → Friction coefficient during releasing (defaults to MUE if not given).

5. Eccentricity & clearances  
   • ECC ([mm], default 0.0)  
     → Maximum tendon offset inside the duct.  
   • CDIS ([mm], default 0.0)  
     → Minimum clearance between adjacent ducts.  
   • CEDG ([mm], default 0.0)  
     → Minimum clearance between a duct and the concrete boundary.

6. Jacking & elongation  
   • SP ([mm], mandatory)  
     → Slip length at the jacking anchor.  
   • SF ([mm], default 0.0)  
     → Additional elongation allowances.  
   • LPRE ([mm], default 0.50)  
     → Straight-length allowance at the jacking anchor.  
   • LFIX ([mm], default = LPRE)  
     → Straight length at the dead anchor (defaults to LPRE).

• For backward compatibility, every value must be preceded by its keyword label in the input file (e.g. “MINR 8.3”).  
• SYSS is a pared‐down version of SYSP for pre-tensioning: it assumes that the installation (ICS1) and grouting (ICS2) phases in the CS record are identical. All the same items appear, but only the simplified subset is needed. A sample SYSS line might read:  
  SYSS NOPS 1 MAT 2 ZV 3898.8 AZ 19*150 LITZ 19 TITL “Pre-tensioning System”  
• The reference force ZV feeds into prestress limit checks (PFAC) and into the ECHO TEND or PLOT FACT reporting routines.

In order to create a geometry for a tendon, a reference axis must be created first. One or more duct curves can then be defined on the reference axis. A duct can then contain one or more tendons.
 The following records are used to generate the geometry:
 AXES The record AXES creates a reference axis on which the stations and optionally spans are defined.
 There are several ways to create a reference axis:
 • Through a sequence of beams or beam nodes.
 • Via structural lines (e.g. SOFiMSHC SLN).
 • Via an existing geometry axis (e.g. SOFiMSHC GAX).
 • Via the input of vertices of a polygon.
 For the plan and elevation drawings, the duct and the intersected elements are unrolled along the reference axis (see PLOT).
 TOPP Using the TOPP record, the reference axis can be divided into individual spans (optional).
 TGEO The record TGEO creates a duct geometry with respect to a reference axis. There are three possibilities to generate a curve:
 • Spline: By specifying constraining points of the type PTUV. Here points and tan- gents are defined with respect to the reference axis through which a spline curve is interpolated. The resulting duct curve follows the curvature of the reference axis.
 • Polygon: By specifying constraining points of the type PTSV. Here, a polygon is defined with respect to the reference axis whose corners can subsequently be rounded via deflection blocks. In contrast to the spline geometry, the edges of the polygon are independent of the curvature of the reference axis, i.e., a straight connection between two constraint points remains straight.
 • Reference: By specifying an already existing duct geometry, analogous to
 AXES.
 PTUV Constraining points of the spline duct geometry. The points are given with respect to the reference axis.
 PTSV Constraining points of the polygonal duct geometry (e.g. for an external tendon). The points are given with respect to the reference axis.

Below is a structured, detailed breakdown of the four parameters (table items) used by the TOPP command when defining top‐positions along a reference axis. This description is intended for ingestion into a RAG‐based vector store and draws on the surrounding context (spans, cantilevers, etc.) to clarify how each field is used.

1. NOH  
   • Name: NOH  
   • Purpose: Identifies which reference axis the TOPP entry belongs to.  
   • Data type / Unit: Integer (no unit)  
   • Default: none (mandatory field)  
   • Comments:  
     – Every TOPP record must specify NOH.  
     – This number ties the station or beam‐node definition back to the correct axis geometry (TGEO).  
     – If you have multiple reference axes in a model, you will use different NOH values to distinguish them.

2. KIND  
   • Name: KIND  
   • Purpose: Determines whether the S‐value refers to an actual beam node or to a station point along the reference axis.  
   • Data type / Allowed values: Four‐character literal (LIT4)  
     – “NODE” = S is measured at a discrete beam node.  
     – “REFX” = S is measured on the reference axis itself (e.g. at supports).  
   • Default: NODE  
   • Comments:  
     – Use NODE when you want the top position pegged exactly at the location of an existing beam node.  
     – Use REFX to subdivide the axis into spans at support locations (even if no physical node is present there).  
     – Each REFX entry effectively creates a new span boundary, length = 1.0 per span.

3. S  
   • Name: S  
   • Purpose: Specifies the coordinate along the reference axis (or beam) at which the top position is created.  
   • Data type / Unit: Real number, [length units consistent with model]  
   • Default: none (mandatory field)  
   • Comments:  
     – If S does not fall exactly on the reference axis (for a NODE‐KIND entry), the nearest axis station is used.  
     – This value is interpreted relative to the axis origin or to the preceding support when used alongside spans.  
     – Example: S=0.4 with KIND=REFX on NOH=1 and SP=1 defines the start of the first span at 0.4 m from the axis origin (a cantilever).

4. SP  
   • Name: SP  
   • Purpose: Defines the span index to which the given S‐coordinate belongs. Controls span creation and ordering.  
   • Data type / Unit: Integer (no unit)  
   • Default: none (mandatory field)  
   • Rules & Comments:  
     – SP must form a strictly ascending sequence (e.g. 0,1,2,… or 1,2,3,…).  
     – The first SP = 0 indicates a cantilever at the start. Otherwise SP1=1 means no cantilever.  
     – A negative final SP (e.g. –4) signals “no cantilever at end”—the last value will be made positive internally.  
     – A positive final SP (e.g. 5) indicates a cantilever beyond the last support.  
     – Once spans are defined, the reference axis is divided exactly once into N spans, each of normalized length 1.0.

How these fields work together  
– In System A (with cantilevers at both ends), you would see:  
    TOPP 1 KIND REFX S 0.0 SP 0     ⇒ start cantilever  
    TOPP 1 KIND REFX S 0.4 SP 1      ⇒ support 1, begin span 1  
    TOPP 1 KIND REFX S 10.0 SP 2     ⇒ support 2, begin span 2  
    …  
    TOPP 1 KIND REFX S 30.4 SP 4     ⇒ support 4, end span 3  
    TOPP 1 KIND REFX S 30.8 SP 5     ⇒ end cantilever  

– In System B (no cantilevers), SP runs 1, 2, 3 and the final SP = –4 is interpreted as end‐of‐span with no overhang. The endpoints at S=0.0 and the axis length (e.g. 5.0 m) are auto‐inserted if not explicitly specified.

Key takeaways for RAG ingestion  
– NOH groups TOPP entries by axis.  
– KIND toggles between “beam node” versus “axis station.”  
– S gives the precise offset along the axis/beam.  
– SP orders these offsets into spans and encodes cantilever logic.

Below is a structured, field-by-field description of the “GRP” attribute table you provided.  This record must appear before any TGEO records and serves to control which element groups (primary or secondary) are active for intersection with duct curves.

1.  Table Columns  
    •  Item  
       – The name of the attribute field.  
    •  Description  
       – A brief explanation of the field’s purpose.  
    •  Unit  
       – The data type or format expected. “LIT4” indicates a 4-character literal; “–” means no unit or free format.  
    •  Default  
       – The value assumed if the field is not supplied.

2.  Field Definitions  

    A.  NO  
        •  Description  
           – Specifies the identifier of the element group to be (de-)activated.  
             You can supply:  
             •  A numeric code (primary group)  
             •  A quoted literal (secondary group)  
             •  The keyword ALL (all groups)  
        •  Unit  
           – “–” (no fixed format) or “LIT4” when using a literal—up to four characters.  
        •  Default  
           – ALL (all groups remain active unless explicitly changed)  

    B.  CMD  
        •  Description  
           – The action to perform on the specified group:  
             •  ON  = enable (activate)  
             •  OFF = disable (deactivate)  
        •  Unit  
           – LIT4 (a four-character literal, e.g. “ON  ” or “OFF ”)  
        •  Default  
           – ON (groups are enabled by default)  

3.  Operational Context and Rules  
    •  This GRP record configures which element groups a subsequent TGEO (duct-curve) record will intersect.  
    •  By default, all defined element groups are active.  
    •  Issuing “GRP NO <group> CMD ON” when no prior ON commands exist resets the active set to that single group. Additional ON/OFF records can add or remove other groups.  
    •  Secondary-group commands (literals) take precedence over primary-group (numeric) commands.  
    •  Using “GRP NO ’ALL’ CMD ON/OFF” resets the entire group control:  
      – CMD ON reactivates every group.  
      – CMD OFF deactivates every group.  

4.  Example Workflows  
    •  Example A: Restrict TGEO 1 to primary groups 100 and 200  
       – GRP NO 100 CMD ON  
       – GRP NO 200 CMD ON  
       – TGEO 1 …  
    •  Example B: Allow TGEO 2 to intersect all groups  
       – GRP NO ’ALL’ CMD ON  
       – TGEO 2 …  
    •  Example C: Exclude secondary group SEC1 from TGEO 3  
       – GRP NO ’SEC1’ CMD OFF  
       – TGEO 3 …

   • Unit: meters  
   • Default: 0 (straight‐through)

6. V  
   • Description: Local vertical offset (local z‐direction) from the origin.  
   • Unit: meters  
   • Default: 0

7. DUS  
   • Description: Inclination (slope) of the constraining curve in the local y–s (horizontal) plane.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: none

8. DVS  
   • Description: Inclination of the curve in the local z–s (vertical) plane.  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: none

9. DL / DR  
   • Description: Lengths of straight‐line “tangent” segments attached to the constraining point along the negative (DL) or positive (DR) s-direction. Over these segments, the duct is enforced straight.  
   • Unit: meters  
   • Default: none

10. RH / RV  
   • Description: Radii of curvature in the horizontal (RH) or vertical (RV) construction plane. The radius is chosen so that adjacent PTUV points join with minimal curvature.  
   • Unit: meters  
   • Default: none

11. RL  
   • Description: “Influence length” of the radius. Overrides the auto-computed radius length. An improper RL may produce sharp “kinks.”  
   • Unit: meters  
   • Default: none

12. KIND  
   • Description: If set, forces a straight connector of system-defined length instead of a curved spline. Two options (LIT4):  
     – PRES: jacking anchor (presumably pre–stressed)  
     – FIX: dead anchor  
   • Default: none (i.e., free spline)

Additional remarks:  
– Unless CSP is used, the local uzv‐coordinate system’s origin is the point S on the reference axis and its y‐axis and z‐axis align with horizontal and vertical planes of the unwrapped axis. In that frame, U moves sideways and V moves vertically.  
– If exactly one PTUV entry uses CSP with S=0.0 (and no other points), the duct is guided continuously through that cross‐section in every beam cross section. Otherwise CSP only affects the given station S.  
– Internally, two planar auxiliary curves (horizontal and vertical) are constructed through these points, then swept/joined into the 3D spline duct.

content:
The table under review documents the syntax and meaning of the PTSV record, which is used to define “constraining points” on a polygonal duct geometry (with bending blocks) for external prestressing tendons. Each PTSV entry is read immediately after a TGEO record and may be repeated to build up an ordered list of points along the duct. In contrast to a spline-based duct (PTUV), PTSV directly connects successive points in 3D space; straight-line segments remain straight even if the reference axis is curved.

Key columns in the table:

• Item  
  – The name of each PTSV parameter: TYPE, S, X, U, V, R, BLCK, KIND.  

• Description  
  – A concise explanation of what the parameter controls in the duct definition.  

• Unit  
  – The unit or data type expected: LIT4 (four-character literal), “–” for dimensionless, or [m] for meters.  

• Default  
  – The value assumed if the parameter is omitted.

Detailed breakdown:

1. TYPE  
   • Defines how the point’s location along the structure is specified.  
   • Valid literals (LIT4):  
     • NODE – the point is placed at an existing beam node.  
     • BEAM – the point lies somewhere along a beam element (requires X).  
     • SPAN – the point is placed at a span position if SPANs were created with TOPP.  
     • REFX – the point is defined by a station coordinate on the reference axis.  
   • Default: BEAM

2. S  
   • The coordinate or index that locates the point according to TYPE.  
   • No units; if TYPE is BEAM, S is the beam number; if NODE, S is the node ID; if REFX, S is the station along the axis; if SPAN, S is the span index.  
   • Default: 0.0

3. X  
   • A relative position along the beam element (only meaningful when TYPE=BEAM).  
   • Unit: meters.  
   • Must lie within [0, bem], where bem is the beam’s length.  
   • Default: 0.0

4. U and V  
   • U: local y-coordinate offset of the point (horizontal deviation).  
   • V: local z-coordinate offset of the point (vertical deviation).  
   • Both in meters, measured in the local coordinate system of the reference axis.  
   • Default: blank (interpreted as zero if omitted).

5. R and BLCK  
   • R: bending radius of the curved transition between adjacent straight segments.  
   • BLCK: length of the bending block that effects that curvature.  
   • Both in meters.  
   • Default R is MINR (the minimum radius defined in the prestressing system SYSP), BLCK default is blank.  
   • Processing rules (see figure 3.10):  
     – If R is blank and BLCK is blank, R defaults to MINR and BLCK is computed.  
     – If R>0 and BLCK is blank, BLCK is determined to fit R≥MINR.  
     – If R is blank and BLCK>0, R defaults to MINR; block is set to BLCK.  
     – If R>0 and BLCK>0 but R<MINR or BLCK too short, R is raised to MINR and/or BLCK recalculated.

6. KIND  
   • If set to PRES (jacking anchor) or FIX (dead anchor), a straight-line segment of fixed length is appended instead of a bend.  
   • The length of that segment is LPRE or LFIX from SYSP.  
   • Literal, default blank (no forced segment).

Additional notes drawn from context:  
• All U, V, R, BLCK and KIND parameters are applied in the local reference frame of the axis (see figure 3.9).  
• The table’s defaults ensure that, unless offsets or bends are explicitly defined, points lie on the reference axis or beam with minimum-radius turns.  
• Typical usage involves a series of PTSV lines such as:  
  PTSV TYPE REFX S 0.0 U 0.0 V –0.5 R – BLCK – KIND FIX  
  PTSV TYPE REFX S 10.0 U 0.0 V  0.5 R 50 BLCK 4 KIND –  
  … etc.  
• See related commands: AXES (coordinate systems), TOPP (span generation), TGEO (duct geometry header), PTUV (spline-based duct).

The illustration shows a cut-away view through a prestressed T-beam and the local coordinate system that is attached to its reference axis. At the very center of the image is point O, the origin of the local system, which lies on the reference axis and coincides with the beam’s cross-section centroid. From O three orthogonal axes emanate:  

• The red X-axis (labelled “x”) is tangent to the reference axis and points along the beam’s length to the right.  
• The green Y-axis (labelled “y”) lies in the plane of the top flange, pointing backward into the page (toward the beam’s support).  
• The blue Z-axis (labelled “z”) is vertical, pointing downward, normal to the flange.  

A prestressing tendon (rendered as an orange rod) enters the beam from the right. As it reaches the interior recess, it bends downward around a duct bend, travels vertically for a short distance, then re-emerges through a second bend and continues horizontally. The beam itself is shaded light gray and shows an interior pocket cut into the web to accommodate this ducting.  

Superimposed on the beam are two dashed construction lines in green (horizontal) and blue (vertical). They mark the local offsets U and V from the origin O to a constraining point on the duct’s centerline. In other words:  
– U is the distance measured in the local y-direction (along the flange) from O to the duct.  
– V is the distance measured in the local z-direction (downward) from O to the duct.  

Together, U and V locate any “constraining point” in the cross-section at a given station S along the reference axis. In the context of polygonal-duct geometry (PTSV entries), each point is defined by its station coordinate S, its U/V offsets, and optional bending parameters (radius R, block length BLCK) or point KIND (PRES for prestress, FIX for fixed anchorage). For example, one might specify:  

• At S = 0.0 m, U = 0.0, V = –0.5 m, KIND = FIX (anchorage point).  
• At S = 10.0 m, U = 0.0, V = +0.5 m, R = 50 mm, BLCK = 4 mm (first bend).  
• …and so on for additional bends and prestressing points.  

Key take-aways from the figure:  
1. The reference axis (not drawn explicitly) runs through O with tangent direction along X.  
2. The local coordinate frame (X, Y, Z) is fixed to the beam, so that duct-layout points can be entered in local U/V offsets without unwrapping the beam in separate horizontal/vertical planes.  
3. Bends in the duct are introduced at constraining points; straight segments remain straight even if the reference axis itself curves in 3D.  

Altogether, Figure 3.9 provides the geometric framework needed to interpret PTSV entries in a prestress tendon layout: it shows how each constraining point’s station S and local offsets (U, V) situate the tendon inside the beam section, and how subsequent bending blocks (radius, length) or straight segments (via KIND flags) are generated along the polygonal duct.

content:
The figure presents a schematic side-view of a polygonal duct’s bending block at the tangent-intersection point (“S”), emphasizing how straight segments connect through a rounded arc of prescribed radius (“R”) and block length (“BLCK”). At the very top, a horizontal dash-dot line denotes the reference axis; directly below it, a vertical dashed line marked “S” indicates the station of the constraining point on that axis. Along this vertical, the distance from the reference axis down to the tangent intersection is labelled “v,” showing the local-coordinate vertical offset (V).

On each side of S, straight red lines represent the incoming and outgoing duct segments. These would, in the absence of a bending block, meet at S with sharp angles; dotted black curves trace how a purely spline-based duct might sweep continuously in both horizontal and vertical planes. Instead, the polygonal approach inserts a blue circular arc between the two red lines. That arc is the bending block itself: its curvature has constant radius R, indicated by an arrow drawn from a point on the arc back up along a blue radial line. Beneath the arc, a horizontal double-arrow dimension labelled “BLCK” defines the block’s length along the duct centerline.

At the left and right ends of the blue arc, the arc meets each straight red segment exactly tangentially—i.e., with matching direction vectors—so the transition is smooth. The combination of straight lines plus this single, constant-radius arc yields a 3D curve that follows the specified constraining points directly, rather than unrolling into separate horizontal and vertical profiles. Captioned “Figure 3.10: Bending block at tangent intersection,” the drawing illustrates how PTSV input parameters (TYPE, REFX/S, U/V offsets, R and BLCK values, KIND) define each constraining point and generate a localized rounded link between straight duct segments without requiring a prior spline fit.

content:
The image presents a schematic “block-diagram” view of how a prestressing tendon is defined in the RAG input data structure. It is enclosed in a dashed “Tendon” frame that shows all records contributing to the definition of a single tendon (TEND). Visually it divides into three logical groups feeding into the central TEND record:

1. Geometry  
   • A single rectangular block labeled “TGEO” sits above the main “TEND” block.  
   • A solid arrow runs downward from TGEO into TEND, indicating that the duct geometry is a mandatory prerequisite for defining a tendon.  

2. Optional Pre‐and Post-Processing Records (left side)  
   • Three rectangles—CS, PDAT, FRIC—are arrayed vertically to the left of TEND.  
   • Each is connected to TEND via a dotted line (indicating these are optional records that may precede TEND).  
     – CS: Construction stages for installation, grouting and removal  
     – PDAT: Prestressing calculation data  
     – FRIC: Friction losses  

3. Stress-Limit Definitions (right side)  
   • Four rectangles—PSIG, PAAS, PFAC, PDEF—stacked vertically to the right of TEND.  
   • Solid lines from each of these blocks point into TEND, indicating that after the TEND record itself, at least one of these must follow to define the prestressing sequence.  
     – PSIG: Stressing limits according to Eurocode  
     – PAAS: Stressing limits according to AASHTO  
     – PFAC: Stressing limits with user-defined factors  
     – PDEF: Manual prestressing sequence  

Beneath the diagram, a small four-column table enumerates the stress-limit parameters provided by PSIG, PAAS and PFAC records:
  • Limit identifier (σp,m; σpm0; σjck; σded)  
  • Corresponding input items (PSIG, PAAS, PFAC)  
  • Factor designation (k1,k2, k3,k4, k5,k6, k7,k8)  
  • Code keyword (FACA, FAC, FACE, FACF)  
  • Description (e.g. Maximum stress during stressing, General stress limit after anchor set, Stress limit at jacking anchor, Stress limit at dead anchor)  

Below the table, a short bullet list clarifies the seven records available to define a tendon in the input deck:
  1. CS – construction stages (optional)  
  2. PDAT – prestress calculation data (optional)  
  3. FRIC – friction losses (optional)  
  4. PSIG – Eurocode stress limits  
  5. PAAS – AASHTO stress limits  
  6. PFAC – stress limits with factors  
  7. PDEF – manual prestressing operations  

Finally, accompanying explanatory text stresses that:
  • TGEO must always precede TEND to supply the duct geometry.  
  • Any CS/PDAT/FRIC records appear before TEND if used.  
  • After TEND, at least one stress-limit record (PSIG, PAAS, PFAC or PDEF) is mandatory to define the prestressing sequence.  
  • Default series properties for subsequent tendons may be overridden on a per-tendon basis.  

Altogether the diagram and tables concisely map out the hierarchy and ordering rules for all input records needed to create and control one prestressing tendon in the RAG model.

The image is a schematic stress–history plot (Figure 3.11 “Prestressing with stress limits”) that illustrates how tendon stress evolves through the main stages of a prestressing operation, and how it is bounded by the four stress limits defined in the table. Visually it combines a red stress-time curve, three blue vertical markers, a pair of horizontal limit lines, and four numbered theoretical trend-lines at the right-hand end.

1. Coordinate system and overall layout  
   • The vertical axis (left) represents tendon stress σ (units not shown). An upward‐pointing arrow at its tip indicates “increasing stress,” and near the bottom is a triangular marker labeled σ_ded (“dead anchor” stress limit).  
   • The horizontal axis represents the sequence of operations (no explicit time or distance units). Directly beneath it is the figure caption: “Figure 3.11: Prestressing with stress limits.”  
   • On the far right is a short, heavy black vertical line that re-plots the final stress axis, now annotated with the four numbered reference points (①, ②, ③, ④).

2. Stress–history (red) curve  
   • Starting at the left, the red curve begins slightly above the dead-anchor limit σ_ded. This is the initial stress in the tendon after installation but before jacking.  
   • It then rises smoothly—and somewhat convexly—through the stressing phase toward the maximum allowable stressing stress σ_p,m.  
   • The apex of the red curve corresponds to the jacking anchor stage. Immediately after this peak, the stress is released from the jack, causing a sudden drop to a lower value.  
   • A short plateau follows, representing the anchor‐set stress.  
   • Beyond the anchor set, the curve dips again (reflecting elastic shortening and friction losses over time), then approaches its final long-term or “service” stress level at the far right.

3. Vertical blue lines (key prestressing events)  
   • The first blue line, aligned with the red‐curve apex, marks the end of active jacking and the maximum stress σ_p,m.  
   • The second blue line, a little to the right, denotes anchor-setting—when the prestressing force is “locked in.”  
   • The third blue line indicates completion of immediate losses (e.g. elastic shortening of concrete and friction), after which only long‐term losses remain.

4. Horizontal stress limits  
   • Midway up the graph is a dashed horizontal line labeled σ_pm0 (the general stress limit after anchor set). In the table on the top right this corresponds to “σ_pm0, k3,k4, k3 FAC.”  
   • The bottom triangle on the left marks σ_ded (dead-anchor stress limit, “σ_ded, k7,k8, k2 FACF”).  
   • The jacking‐anchor limit σ_jck and the maximum stressing limit σ_p,m (with factors k1,k2) are implied by the peak of the red curve but not drawn explicitly as lines.

5. Theoretical post-loss trend lines (numbered ①–④ on the right)  
   • ① (solid, steepest upward) shows the idealized maximum‐stress ramp if no limits intervened.  
   • ② (dashed, shallowest) is the extrapolated final stress if ultimate losses were the only effect.  
   • ③ (dotted) represents the stress if one applied the “general post‐set” limit σ_pm0 right after anchoring, then continued loading.  
   • ④ (solid red, circled) is the actual achieved tendon stress at the end of immediate losses, tracing the real prestressing history.

6. Table of limits (top right)  
   The adjacent table summarizes the four stress limits, each with its code, factor group, and description:  
   • σ_p,m  (k1,k2; FACA) – Maximum stress during stressing (jacking anchor)  
   • σ_pm0 (k3,k4; FAC)  – General stress limit after anchor set  
   • σ_jck (k5,k6; FACE) – Stress limit at jacking anchor  
   • σ_ded (k7,k8; FACF) – Stress limit at dead anchor  

Contextually, this plot would be generated from a tendon definition (TEND) laid inside a duct geometry (TGEO). The geometric eccentricity (SYSP ECC) and the length over which the tendon runs inside the duct determine friction and curvature losses, which in turn shape the red stress curve between the jacking peak and the final service level. This figure thus encapsulates, in one view, the interplay of mechanical loading stages and the codified stress‐limit checks that ensure safe prestressing design.

The table titled “Table 3.19: Input items for stress limits” defines four distinct stress‐limit categories for a tendon within its duct geometry.  Each row associates a symbolic limit (σ…), the keys by which its numerical values are read from PSIG and PAAS tables, the family of stress‐factors (PFAC), and a human‐readable description of when that limit applies.  In context, these limits are eventually applied to account for eccentricity (SYSP ECC) and for whether the tendon spans an entire duct or only a section.

Columns  
• Limit – the symbol used in subsequent calculations to identify the particular stress limit.  
• PSIG – a pair of indices (k #) that select the pre‐configured “PSIG” (pre‐stress‐intensity) values.  
• PAAS – an index (k #) into the “PAAS” (post‐anchor‐set) parameters.  
• PFAC – a four‐character family code indicating which set of stress‐factors to use.  
• Description – a concise English label stating the loading stage or anchorage condition under which that limit becomes active.

1. Limit = σₚ,ₘ  
   • PSIG = k₁, k₂  
   • PAAS = k₁  
   • PFAC = “FACA”  
   • Description = “Maximum stress during stressing”  
   • Notes: This is the peak allowable tendon stress when tensioning is in progress, before any load losses or end‐anchorage effects are applied.

2. Limit = σₚₘ₀  
   • PSIG = k₃, k₄  
   • PAAS = k₃  
   • PFAC = “FAC”  
   • Description = “General stress limit after anchor set”  
   • Notes: Used once the anchor has been set and initial elastic shortening and friction losses have occurred; it establishes the upper bound for the stabilized prestress.

3. Limit = σⱼck  
   • PSIG = k₅, k₆  
   • PAAS = k₂  
   • PFAC = “FACE”  
   • Description = “Stress limit at jacking anchor”  
   • Notes: This governs the stress allowed at the jacking end, taking into account specific conditions (e.g. strand seating, local bearing) at that anchor.

4. Limit = σded  
   • PSIG = k₇, k₈  
   • PAAS = k₂  
   • PFAC = “FACF”  
   • Description = “Stress limit at dead anchor”  
   • Notes: Applies to the non‐jacking (dead) end anchor, often different because that end does not experience the same reversal or release phenomena as the jacking side.

Usage and Workflow  
– During model setup, the user supplies numeric tables PSIG and PAAS, each indexed by the k-numbers listed above.  
– The PFAC code tells the solver which family of adjustment factors to apply (e.g. friction, wobble, seating losses) when computing the actual stress result.  
– The four σ-limits are then enforced at their respective stages or anchor locations.  
– Because the tendon geometry (TEND) may be offset from the duct axis (TGEO) by an eccentricity (SYSP ECC) and can cover the full duct or only a subsection, these stress limits ensure that stresses remain within allowable bounds throughout construction and service life.

A tendon TEND is defined on an duct geometry TGEO. The geometric difference between the tendon geometry and the duct geometry results from the eccentricity of the tendon (SYSP ECC) and the length – the tendon can be defined over the entire duct or only on a section.

The table you’ve provided documents the “CS” attribute record, which must appear before any “TEND” definition in your input deck. Its purpose is to assign integer stage numbers to the three primary phases of tendon handling—installation, grouting and removal—and to supply an optional textual title for these stages. Below is a detailed breakdown of each column and row:

1. Record context  
   • Record name: CS (Construction Stages)  
   • Positioning: Must be declared prior to any TEND records in the file.  
   • Related records: PDAT, PSIG, PAAS, PFAC, PDEF, FRIC, TEND.

2. Columns  
   • Item: The internal keyword for each parameter in the CS record.  
   • Description: A natural‐language explanation of what the parameter controls.  
   • Unit: The expected data type or measurement unit; for these stage indicators, this is blank (integer index) or, in one case, a literal‐string type.  
   • Default: The value assumed when the parameter is not explicitly provided.

3. Rows / Items  

   a) ICS1 – “Construction stage installation”  
      – Unit: (none)  
      – Default: 1  
      – Purpose: Specifies the stage number at which the tendon is installed. If you omit ICS1, the system assumes the installation occurs at stage 1.  

   b) ICS2 – “Construction stage grouting”  
      – Unit: (none)  
      – Default: ICS1  
      – Purpose: Specifies the stage at which grout is injected around the tendon. By default it inherits the same stage as installation (i.e. ICS2 = ICS1). If the tendon does not require grouting—common for external tendon systems—you may set ICS2 to “NONE” or the numeric sentinel 9999.  

   c) ICS3 – “Construction stage removal”  
      – Unit: (none)  
      – Default: 0  
      – Purpose: Defines the stage at which the tendon is removed. A value of zero (0) indicates that the tendon is never removed. To schedule removal, assign a positive integer stage number here.  

   d) TITL – “Title of the construction stages”  
      – Unit: LIT32 (up to 32 characters literal string)  
      – Default: none (no automatic title)  
      – Purpose: Provides a human‐readable name for the set of construction stages. Enclose the title in quotation marks.

4. Usage examples  
   • CS ICS1 11 ICS2 NONE ICS3 0 TITL “Construction stages”  
     – Install at stage 11, omit grouting, do not remove, and label the sequence “Construction stages.”  
   • CS ICS1 11 ICS2 12 ICS3 @ TITL “Construction stages”  
     – Install at stage 11, grout at stage 12, leave ICS3 undefined (symbol “@”), and apply the same title.

By explicitly specifying these four CS parameters, you ensure that subsequent TEND records will correctly reference the intended installation, grouting and removal phases under a clear descriptive heading.

The table defines six parameters used in the PDAT attribute record of a prestressing‐tendon definition (TEND) and must always appear before the TEND record in the input deck.  PDAT is an umbrella record that historically contained more fields than are now documented; to preserve backward compatibility each field’s name must always precede its value (for example “AR 2000”).  Several of these parameters feed directly into crack‐width checks and force‐transition modeling whenever tendons are not fully anchored or when partial‐loss slip behavior must be represented.

1.  FTL (Force‐Transition Length)  
   • Description: Specifies the length over which the tendon transitions load when no mechanical anchor is present.  In practice this models how prestress is transferred into the surrounding concrete by bond.  If a slip event occurs, this length is used to compute the zone that must be checked for local stresses.  
   • Unit: meters [m]  
   • Default: 0.00 (i.e. no transition length unless explicitly provided)  

2.  FTYP (Force‐Transition Type)  
   • Description: Selects the shape of the force‐transfer curve over the FTL zone.  Six options are available:  
     – LINE:  linear variation on both ends of the tendon  
     – PARA:  parabolic variation on both ends  
     – LLIN: linear on the left end only, constant on the right end  
     – RLIN: linear on the right end only, constant on the left end  
     – LPAR: parabolic on the left end only  
     – RPAR: parabolic on the right end only  
   • Unit code: LIT4 (four‐character literal)  
   • Default: LINE  

   These settings control how internal tendon forces ramp up (or down) in the region defined by SFRO/STO in the TEND record.

3.  MATA (Material‐Subtract ID)  
   • Description: Identifies an auxiliary material whose properties should be subtracted from the cross‐section.  Use only when the cross‐section material differs from that of the tendon profile.  
   • Unit: none (integer identifier)  
   • Default: none (field may be omitted if subtracted‐material ID is identical to section material)  

4.  AR (Reference Area for Crack‐Width Design)  
   • Description: The effective area, in square millimeters, used when estimating crack widths around the tendon.  This area often equals the sum of individual strand areas or the total steel area in a multi‐strand duct.  
   • Unit: mm²  
   • Default: user‐calculated (“*” placeholder); if not provided the software assumes  
     AR = cross‐section area AZ multiplied by the number of tendons NTEN.  

5.  UZ (Circumference of Tendon for Crack‐Width)  
   • Description: The effective perimeter (in millimeters) over which tension is transferred to the surrounding concrete.  This is used in crack‐width formulas that relate bond stress to crack opening.  
   • Unit: mm  
   • Default: “*”; if omitted a default value of (VAZ · NTEN) is assumed, where VAZ is the nominal circumference per tendon.  

6.  DZ (Effective Diameter)  
   • Description: Diameter (in millimeters) representing the tendon core, including grout or sheath if relevant, used for strength and stiffness checks.  
   • Unit: mm  
   • Default: “*”; user must supply or fall back on section‐material defaults.  

Remarks and Cross‐References  
•  Because AR, UZ and DZ all refer to the total number of tendons NTEN, omissions will trigger internal defaults based on AZ, VAZ and NTEN (see the AQB manual for full formulas).  
•  The PDAT record feeds into the TEND definition, so FTL/FTYP must appear before listing individual tendon segments.  
•  See also related prestress records: CS (cross‐section), PSIG (prestress loads), PAAS (anchor stresses), PFAC (force factors), PDEF (prestress definitions), FRIC (friction), and TEND (tendon geometry).

The table presented defines the five parameters of the FRIC record, an attribute‐only record used to introduce or modify localized friction effects in a tendon system.  In practice the FRIC record must appear before any TEND definitions in your input deck; if it appears with no numerical arguments, all custom friction settings revert to their built-in defaults.  Internally, these values are treated exactly like the SYSP BETA and BETG inputs and do not alter tendon geometry—they simply superimpose extra “wobble” (frictional loss) onto the existing system.

Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1.  FROM  
    – Description: “Station of the start of the friction.”  
    – Unit: none (this is a nondimensional chainage or station index along the tendon path).  
    – Default: 0  
    – Remarks: If you omit FROM, the extra friction begins at station 0.

2.  TO  
    – Description: “Station with the end of friction.”  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: 0  
    – Remarks: Together, FROM and TO define the continuous segment over which the additional friction applies.  If TO ≤ FROM, effectively no segment is defined and no extra friction is applied.

3.  BETA  
    – Description: “Additional wobble at the begin.”  
    – Unit: [deg/m] (degrees per meter) – quantifies frictional loss per unit length at the start of the zone.  
    – Default: 0  
    – Remarks: This is the magnitude of extra “angular misalignment” per meter added to whatever baseline friction the system already has at station FROM.

4.  BETE  
    – Description: “Additional wobble at the end.”  
    – Unit: [deg/m]  
    – Default: same as BETA  
    – Remarks: Allows tapering the added friction between the start and the end stations.  If you omit BETE, it is assumed equal to BETA (constant friction over the zone).

5.  TYPE  
    – Description: “Type of superposition.”  Two modes are supported:  
      • ADD: additive superposition (β_total = β_exist + β_add)  
      • VECT: vectorial superposition (β_total = sqrt(β_exist² + β_add²))  
    – Unit: LIT4 (literal string)  
    – Default: ADD  
    – Remarks:  
        ­– ADD simply accumulates the existing friction angle with the extra angle.  
        ­– VECT combines them in a root-sum-square fashion, which can be more physically representative when friction sources act independently in orthogonal directions.

Usage example (from the context section):  
“FRIC FROM 10.0 TO 15.0 BETA 0.005[1/m] TYPE ADD”  

This will insert an additional 0.005 deg/m of friction over the tendon path between stations 10 and 15, adding linearly to whatever friction was already present.  

See also related records: CS, PDAT, PSIG, PAAS, PFAC, PDEF, TEND.
