The table shown is the definition of the PSIG attribute record, which must appear before any TEND record in a prestressing input deck. PSIG overwrites previously set PFAC, PSIG, PAAS or PDEF records and – in the case of two-sided prestressing – may be repeated to define a different sequence for the second side. Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1. Item: KIND  
   • Description: Type of prestressing, i.e. from which end the tendon is jacked.  
     – “RI” : Prestressing from the right end  
     – “LE” : Prestressing from the left end  
     – “RILE”: First from right, then from left (two-sided)  
     – “LERI”: First from left, then from right (two-sided)  
   • Unit: LIT4 (4-character literal)  
   • Default: RI  

2. Item: ANWS  
   • Description: Sequence of operations applied to the tendon. Each of the four operations can be combined by literal or by bit-mask:  
     – 1 or T = Stressing (initial jacking)  
     – 2 or R = Releasing (secondary)  
     – 4 or W = Re-stressing (re-jacking)  
     – 8 or S = Slip (final anchorage slip)  
     By default, ANWS = “TS” (stressing followed by slip). Equivalently, 1 + 8 = 9 can be used.  
   • Unit: LIT4 or numeric mask  
   • Default: TS  

3. Items: KAPA and KAPL  
   • KAPA (κ): Safety friction factor κ to reduce the jacking force and prevent overstress. If omitted, it is set per the national annex; 0.0 disables friction safety; values outside the permissible range are reset to the annex value.  
   • KAPL: Defines the influence length of κ when tensioning from both ends:  
     – SYMM: Symmetrical reduction (both sides see the same κ-based reduction)  
     – OPT: Optimised reduction (second side considers only the portion under additional force; may revert to SYMM if unsolvable)  
   • Unit for both: LIT4 (for KAPL) / dimensionless (for KAPA)  
   • Default: KAPA = (annex value), KAPL = SYMM  

4. Items: K1, K2, K3, K4  
   • These four k-values set stress limits in two phases, based on Eurocode conventions:  
     – K1 and K2 control the maximum prestress σp,max during jacking as σp,max = min(k1·fpk, k2·fp0,1k)  
     – K3 and K4 control the general stress limit after anchor set: σpm0 = min(k3·fpk, k4·fp0,1k)  
   • Interpretation of numeric entries:  
     – If k < 10, the value is treated as a factor of the characteristic strengths fpk or fp0,1k  
     – If k ≥ 10, the value is used directly as a stress limit (and its counterpart is ignored)  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless or stress depending on context)  
   • Default: Taken from the applicable national annex or standard  

5. Items: K5, K6, K7, K8  
   • These secondary k-values (numbered differently from Eurocode) can directly override stress limits at specific anchors:  
     – K5: Factor for stress limit at the jacking anchor (used as K3 if omitted)  
     – K6: Analogous factor for σjack = min(k5·fpk, k6·fp0,1k) (defaults to K4 if omitted)  
     – K7: Factor for stress limit at the dead anchor (defaults to K3)  
     – K8: Analogous for σdead = min(k7·fpk, k8·fp0,1k) (defaults to K4)  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless or stress)  
   • Default: Inherited from K3/K4 where indicated  

Remarks and Usage Notes:  
- PSIG must precede TEND.  
- If prestressing is performed from both ends, a second PSIG record can redefine only ANWS; k-values and KAPA/KAPL remain as originally set.  
- For direct manual stress or force inputs, use the PDEF record instead.  
- The table’s numbering of k-values (1–8) differs slightly from the Eurocode notation for historical reasons.

Below is a detailed, field-by-field description of the prestressing attribute table. This table corresponds to the PAAS record in the input syntax and must be specified before the TEND record. It replaces any previously set PFAC, PSIG, PAAS or PDEF attributes. If you need two-sided prestressing with a different sequence on the second side, issue a second PAAS record: only the ANWS value is updated; the K-values carry over.

Fields:

1. Item: KIND  
   • Description: Defines the direction and order of prestressing.  
   • Allowed values (unit LIT4):  
     – RI   : Prestressing from right  
     – LE   : Prestressing from left  
     – RILE : First from right, then left (two-sided)  
     – LERI : First from left, then right (two-sided)  
   • Default: RI  

2. Item: ANWS  
   • Description: Specifies the prestressing sequence. You can either combine literal codes or use their numeric bitmask equivalents.  
     – Literals:  
       T (Stressing)  
       R (Releasing)  
       W (Re-stressing)  
       S (Slip)  
     – Bitmask:  
       1 = T, 2 = R, 4 = W, 8 = S  
       e.g. “TS” → 1 + 8 = 9, “TRW” → 1 + 2 + 4 = 7  
   • Unit: LIT4 / –  
   • Default: TS  

3. Item: K1  
   • Description: Stress limit prior to seating (maximum strand stress before initial wedge seating).  
     – σ_max = k1 · f_py  (equivalently k1 · f_p0,1k)  
   • Unit: dimensionless multiplier  
   • Default: (mandatory) – indicated by “!”  

4. Item: K2  
   • Description: Stress limit at the anchorages.  
     – σ_anchor = k2 · f_pu  (equivalently k2 · f_pk)  
   • Unit: dimensionless multiplier  
   • Default: (mandatory) – indicated by “!”  

5. Item: K3  
   • Description: General stress limit after the anchor set is completed.  
     – σ_sconst = k3 · f_pu  (equivalently k3 · f_pk)  
   • Unit: dimensionless multiplier  
   • Default: (mandatory) – indicated by “!”  

Remarks and Usage Notes:  
• The PAAS record must appear before the TEND record in your input deck.  
• It overrides any PFAC, PSIG, PAAS or PDEF attributes previously defined.  
• If you want to specify a different prestressing sequence on the second side in two-sided prestressing, issue a second PAAS line with the new ANWS value. Only ANWS changes; K1–K3 remain as originally set.  
• Values for the K-factors are mandatory (“!”) and must be provided by the user. Typical example:  
  PAAS KIND RILE ANWS 9 K1 0.9 K2 0.7 K3 0.74  
• You may alternatively supply ANWS in bitmask form or literal form (e.g. ANWS 15 is equivalent to T+R+W+S).  

See Also: CS, PDAT, FRIC, PSIG, PFAC, PDEF, TEND.

content:
This record (PFAC) defines the prestressing-force attributes for tendons in a structural model. It must appear before the TEND record and will override any previously set PFAC, PSIG, PAAS or PDEF attributes. In two-sided prestressing a second PFAC can follow to describe the opposite side with its own sequence (ANWS) and force factors (FAC…).

Key points and usage notes  
•  Always label each factor by name (e.g. “FACE 0.95”) – older versions stored undocumented fields, so explicit naming ensures compatibility.  
•  ANWS controls the sequence of operations (stress, release, re-stress, slip) via letters (T, R, W, S) or a bit-mask integer (1, 2, 4, 8; sum of bits).  
•  FAC, FACA, FACE and FACF scale against the reference force ZV defined in the SYSP record.  

Table of PFAC items  

1. KIND (LIT4)  
   - Defines the direction and order of prestressing pulls  
   - Values:  
     • “RI”  – from right side only  
     • “LE”  – from left side only  
     • “RILE”– right first, then left  
     • “LERI”– left first, then right  
   - Default: RI  

2. ANWS (LIT4/–)  
   - Specifies the prestressing sequence as a string of letters or sum of bit flags:  
     • 1 or T → Stressing  
     • 2 or R → Releasing  
     • 4 or W → Re-stressing  
     • 8 or S → Slip (anchor slippage)  
   - Example: “TS” = T(1)+S(8)=9 → stress then slip  
   - Default: TS  

3. FAC (−)  
   - General force factor applied after the anchor has set  
   - Scales the reference force ZV  
   - Default: 1.05  

4. FACA (−)  
   - Maximum force factor allowed during the tensioning operation  
   - Controls upper bound of applied force  
   - Default: 1.18  

5. FACE (−)  
   - Factor applied at the jacking anchor itself  
   - Default: uses FAC’s value if not specified explicitly  

6. FACF (−)  
   - Factor applied at the dead anchor (far end)  
   - Default: uses FAC’s value if not specified explicitly  

Examples  
• Single-side, right-only stressing with default limits:  
  PFAC KIND RI ANWS TS FAC 1.0 FACA 1.1 FACE 0.9 FACF 0.9  
• Overriding one numeric digit using “@” placeholder:  
  PFAC KIND RI ANWS TS FAC 1.@ FACA 1.1 FACE 0.9 FACF @.9  
• Two-sided prestressing with different sequences/limits per side:  
  PFAC KIND RILE ANWS 15 FAC 1.0 FACA 1.1 FACE 0.9 FACF 0.9  
  PFAC KIND RILE ANWS 9  FAC 1.05 FACA 1.18 FACE 1.0 FACF 1.0  

See also related records: CS, PDAT, FRIC, PSIG, PAAS, PDEF, TEND.

The PDEF record defines the prestressing‐step attributes for a structural element and must appear before any TEND (tensioning end) record.  It overrides any previous PFAC, PSIG, PAAS or PDEF definitions.  In what follows, “right” refers to prestressing from the right end of the element; “left” to prestressing from the left end.

1. General Layout  
   • Items (rows) are:  
     – KIND  (the overall prestressing sequence/type)  
     – STR, RER, RSR, SLR  (right-end operations)  
     – STL, REL, RSL, SLL  (left-end operations)  
   • Columns are:  
     – Description  (textual meaning of the item)  
     – Unit  (physical units: force in kN or elongation/ slip in mm)  
     – Default  (value assumed if item is omitted; all zero except KIND)

2. KIND (LIT4, default “RI”)  
   A four-character literal selecting the prestressing strategy:  
     • “RI”   – Prestressing exclusively from the right end  
     • “LE”   – Prestressing exclusively from the left end  
     • “RILE” – First from the right, then from the left  
     • “LERI” – First from the left, then from the right  

3. Right-End Parameters  
   • STR (Right stressing)  
   • RER (Right releasing)  
   • RSR (Right re-stressing)  
   • SLR (Right slip)  

4. Left-End Parameters  
   • STL (Left stressing)  
   • REL (Left releasing)  
   • RSL (Left re-stressing)  
   • SLL (Left slip)  

   – Units for all eight: [kN] when interpreted as a force, or [mm] when interpreted as an elongation/slip length.  – Defaults: 0.  

5. Interpretation of Numeric Values  
   • < 0.0 (negative): treated as a physical length (elongation or release length) or slip amount in millimeters.  
   • = 0.0: the corresponding prestressing step is deactivated (no action).  
   • In the interval ]0.0, 2.0]: treated as a factor multiplying the reference force ZV defined in the SYSP record.  
   • > 2.0: treated directly as a jacking force in kilonewtons.

6. Typical Usage Examples  
   a) Length‐controlled prestressing (pure elongation/slip):  
      PDEF KIND=RILE STR=–80 SLR=–4 STL=–20 SLL=–4  
      (Right first: elongate –80 mm, slip  –4 mm; then left: elongate –20 mm, slip –4 mm.)  
   b) Force‐controlled prestressing:  
      PDEF KIND=RILE STR=2000 SLR=1800 STL=2000 SLL=1800  
      (Apply 2 000 kN stressing, then release/slip 1 800 kN on each side in turn.)  
   c) Factor‐controlled prestressing:  
      PDEF KIND=RILE STR=1.0 SLR=0.9 STL=1.0 SLL=0.9  
      (Use 100 % of reference ZV for stressing, 90 % for releasing/slip.)  
   d) Mixed control:  
      PDEF KIND=RILE STR=2000 SLR=–4 STL=1.0 SLL=–4  
      (Right stressing by force, right slip as length, left stressing as factor, left slip length.)

7. Cross References  
   See also: CS, PDAT, FRIC, PSIG, PAAS, PFAC, TEND.

By following this schema, any downstream RAG‐based retrieval can unambiguously interpret the user’s prestress specification—whether it’s length-based, force-based, factor-based, or a combination thereof—along with the sequencing dictated by KIND.

The table shown documents the parameters of the “TEND” record, which is used to define and activate prestressing tendons along a duct geometry (TGEO) and to trigger friction‐loss calculations in a structural analysis.  All of its fields must be supplied in the correct sequence, and most have a prescribed default value if not explicitly set.  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown, including units, defaults, and their roles in the friction and prestress workflow:

1. NOT  
   • Description: Identifier of the tendon. This is a mandatory unique integer.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: “!” (no default; must be specified)  

2. NOG  
   • Description: Identifier of the duct geometry to which this tendon belongs (TGEO record). Also mandatory.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: “!” (no default; must be specified)  

3. NTEN  
   • Description: Number of identical tendons summarized by this single definition. When NTEN > 1, friction is computed for one representative tendon and results multiplied by NTEN.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 1  

4. TYPE  
   • Description: Reference system for specifying the tendon’s “FROM” and “TO” locations. Options (LIT4):  
     – NODE   : beam node numbers (beams only)  
     – BEAM   : beam element numbers  
     – REFX   : stations along the reference axis  
     – SPAN   : span indices defined via TOPP  
   • Unit: LIT4  
   • Default: REFX  

5. FROM  
   • Description: Start location of the tendon, expressed according to TYPE (e.g. node ID, beam ID, station, span). If omitted, defaults to the duct’s start.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: * (duct start)  

6. TO  
   • Description: End location of the tendon, analogous to FROM. If omitted, defaults to the duct’s end.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: * (duct end)  

7. SFRO  
   • Description: Station increment applied to FROM, shifting the actual friction‐analysis start. Positive or negative depending on reference‐axis direction.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 0.00  

8. STO  
   • Description: Station increment applied to TO, shifting the actual friction‐analysis end. Usually negative.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 0.00  

9. EFRO  
   • Description: Offset added to (FROM + SFRO) to define where prestressing force actually becomes effective in the structure.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 0.00  

10. ETO  
   • Description: Offset added to (TO + STO) to define where prestressing force effectiveness ends.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 0.00  

11. LC  
   • Description: Load‐case number under which the computed tendon forces are stored for later use (e.g. in ASE). A value > 0 activates result storage.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: 0  

12. LC0  
   • Description: For beam tendons only: if LC0 ≠ LC and both > 0, the unconstrained prestress forces (no external loads or supports) are also computed and stored under LC0.  
   • Unit: ―  
   • Default: LC  

13. TITL  
   • Description: Descriptive title of the tendon, up to 32 characters.  
   • Unit: LIT32  
   • Default: “–” (empty)  

14. GUID  
   • Description: Globally-unique 128-bit code in hexadecimal, used for database tracking.  
   • Unit: LIT36  
   • Default: “–” (empty)  

Contextual notes:  
• The TEND record must follow definitions of cross‐section (CS), prestress data (PDAT), friction law (FRIC), prestress signal (PSIG), anchor area (PAAS), friction factor (PFAC), and prestress definition (PDEF).  
• Elastic shortening effects are not included in the friction computation.  
• If no eccentricity is set in the prestressing system (SYSP ECC 0), the tendon path coincides with the duct geometry.  
• The maximum tendon length cannot exceed its duct; out‐of‐range FROM/TO coordinates are automatically clipped.  

Example excerpts (using REFX):  
 TEND NOT 202 NOG 102 TYPE REFX  
   FROM 0.0 SFRO 1.0 EFRO 1.0  
   TO 12.0 STO –1.0 ETO –1.0  
   LC 1 TITL "Main Tendon"  

This structured layout makes it straightforward to index and retrieve each tendon parameter for a retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) vector store or any downstream preprocessing.

The illustration (Figure 3.13) shows a longitudinal section through a prestressed flat slab, highlighting the “free tendon layout” option. The slab is rendered as a thick, light-gray rectangular block whose top and bottom surfaces lie parallel to the global XY-plane. A single tendon path is shown in red, weaving between top-layer support points and internally generated mid-span points at the lower layer.

Key geometric and notation elements in the drawing are:

• Slab boundaries and datum offsets  
  – ZSPT: the vertical distance from the global top slab face down to the tendon’s support (top­layer) elevation. This is shown as a short double-headed arrow at the left.  
  – ZSPB: the vertical offset from the global bottom slab face up to the tendon’s lowest layer (midspan) elevation, indicated with another short double-headed arrow on the left.  

• Tendon control points (record type BIT in SLBS):  
  – Bit 4 (left end start point): a white disc located on the left face of the slab at the top layer (ZSPT).  
  – Bit 1 (intermediate support point): a white disc on the top surface, located approximately one third along the slab’s length.  
  – Automatically generated midspan points (not explicitly input by the user): these lie at the lower elevation (ZSPB) roughly midway between support points. They are connected by dashed black lines to the support points.  
  – Bit 8 + 1 (right end support point and tendon exit): a white disc on the right face at the top layer.  

• Span segmentation and tendon length parameters:  
  – FRLT: the length of the end approach regions on both left and right sides, measured from the slab’s vertical face to the first support point. Shown twice above the slab as “FRLT.”  
  – FRLL: the length of the main span segments between successive support points. Two equal FRLL segments are drawn centrally, indicating that the main tendon run is divided into two identical spans.  
  – The overall slab length is therefore 2 × FRLT + 2 × FRLL.  

• Tendon profile:  
  – The solid red curve depicts the actual tendon drape profile, which deviates smoothly between top-layer support points and lower mid-span points.  
  – The dashed black lines represent straight-line chord connections between support and mid-span control points. These define the baseline for curvature checks and duct fabrication.  
  – A thin, dashed horizontal line at mid-thickness indicates the mean QUAD element thickness, used as reference for specifying tendon elevations as edge distances.  

• Supports: two triangular support symbols under the slab—one situated under the left mid-span, the other under the right end—indicate bearing locations of the slab on columns or walls.  

In free tendon layout mode, the engineer only specifies the support points (top-layer anchor positions). All intermediate (mid-span) tendon points at the bottom layer are generated automatically by the system, ensuring the tendon remains within the specified upper and lower edge-distance limits. Internally, the slab tendon model is transformed into the PTUV spline-duct representation for analysis, but the user’s SLAB and SLBS records need only define the general tendon settings and the support-point coordinates in plan and elevation.

The figure shows a schematic cross-section of a flat slab with a single prestressing tendon laid out in spline geometry (analogous to the PTUV duct input). Everything—including plan geometry and tendon elevations—is assumed parallel to the global XY-plane. The slab is drawn as a long, horizontal, gray-filled rectangle. Its top face lies on the elevation line labeled “ZSPT,” and its bottom face on “ZSPB.” Both ZSPT and ZSPB are drawn as fine horizontal lines just outside the slab, with small vertical ticks marking their height.  

Centered inside the slab, a continuous solid blue curve traces the actual tendon path. Externally, a dashed black straight line connects the same sequence of key points, illustrating how the spline path deviates from chord‐to‐chord. There are five white‐filled circles (open markers) along the curve, each denoting a “constraining point” of the tendon:  
 • At the leftmost end of the slab, a circle sits on the top face (start point).  
 • Moving rightward, a second circle marks the first support point, also on the top face.  
 • At about midspan, a third circle sits on the bottom face (midspan point).  
 • Continuing right, a fourth circle marks the second support point on the top face.  
 • Finally, a fifth circle at the far right again touches the top face (end point).  

Below the slab outline, two small filled‐triangle symbols pinpoint the locations of slab supports (columns or bearings)—one beneath the first support point and one beneath the right end. A horizontal arrow at the bottom indicates the positive X-direction. Directly under the slab, a one-row “BIT” coding bar shows integer values at the same five horizontal positions:

These BIT values classify each constraining point according to the record definition (see the BIT parameter in the SLBS record).  

Between the central support points, two short horizontal dimension bars—labeled “DL” (left half-span) and “DR” (right half-span)—indicate the plan‐view distances from the first support to midspan (DL) and from midspan to the second support (DR).  

Captioned as “Figure 3.14: Slab prestressing with spline geometry (analogous to PTUV). The bit describes the type of point (see BIT),” the drawing makes clear how the SLBS input record captures both support (top) points and midspan (bottom) points for a spline tendon layout. Internally, the system will convert this spline description into an equivalent PTUV definition. Continuous tendon curvature is thus controlled by the selected constraining points, their elevations (edge distances measured from the mean slab thickness), and the BIT codes that tell the solver whether a point is a start, end, support or midspan.

For prestressing flat slabs, there is an alternative input of tendons with the records SLAB and SLBS.
 The prerequisite is that the position of the tendons in the plan view is known. With SLAB and SLBS the missing data for the elevation – heights and inclinations – are then added. The plan geometry can be generated with SOFiMSHC or graphically with SOFiPLUS.
 The following rules apply:
 • The slab is parallel to the global XY-plane.
 • The plan geometry is parallel to the global XY-plane and already exists as an axis in the database.
 • Tendon heights are given as edge distances in relation to the mean slab thickness of the QUAD elements.

 Spline geometry: For the spline geometry the input is analogous to PTUV. Both support and midspan points are to be entered (see Figure 3.14).
 Internally, the model is always converted to PTUV. The system created in this way can be exported to a separate file with ECHO SLAB FULL.

The table in question defines the parameters available on the SLAB record, which is used to create a new slab tendon in a prestressed‐concrete model.  SLAB itself establishes the tendon reference and type; subsequent SLBS records define the actual support and span stations that determine tendon geometry.  The table is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and each row corresponds to one SLAB input field.  Below is a detailed walkthrough:

1.  Item column  
    •  Lists the short code for each SLAB field (e.g. NOT, REFS, TYPG, ZSPT, FRLT, etc.).  
    •  Codes in bold blue (ZSPT, ZSPB, FRLT, FRLL) highlight parameters tied to tendon‐layer heights and tendon routing segments.

2.  Description column  
    •  Explains the purpose of each SLAB field.  
    •  Many descriptions reference related records or other commands (for example, “sieht TEND” for LC, or “analogous to PTUV” for TYPG).

3.  Unit column  
    •  Specifies the expected unit type. If a dash (—) appears, the field is dimensionless or uses an internal code.  
    •  Typical units: [m] for lengths (ZSPT, ZSPB, FRLT, FRLL), LIT4 for a 4‐character literal (REFS), LIT32 for a 32‐character literal (TITL).

4.  Default column  
    •  Gives the default value assigned when the field is omitted.  
    •  An exclamation mark (!) indicates the field is mandatory. A minus sign (–) means no default is applied but omission may be allowed.  

Detailed field descriptions:

•  NOT (Number of tendon)  
   –  Defines the tendon index, i.e. the reference axis number and duct geometry number.  
   –  Dimensionless.  
   –  Mandatory (!).

•  REFS (Reference to plan geometry)  
   –  Links this tendon to a plan‐geometry record by its four‐character name.  
   –  Unit: LIT4.  
   –  Mandatory (!).

•  NOPS (Number of prestressing system)  
   –  Identifies which prestressing system the tendon belongs to.  
   –  Dimensionless.  
   –  Mandatory (!).

•  TYPG (Type of geometry generation)  
   –  Options: PTFV (or 1) for free‐tendon layout, PTUV (or 2) for spline geometry analog to PTUV record.  
   –  Unit: – / LIT4.  
   –  Default: PTFV.

•  ICS1, ICS2, ICS3 (Construction stages)  
   –  ICS1: installation stage; ICS2: grouting stage; ICS3: removal stage.  
   –  All are dimensionless with default value 1.

•  S0 (Start station on the plan geometry)  
   –  Defines the longitudinal offset on the REFS curve where this tendon begins.  
   –  Dimensionless station (same units as plan geometry).  
   –  Default: 0.00.

•  ZSPT, ZSPB (Support and span elevations)  
   –  ZSPT: height of tendon supports measured from the upper concrete edge (upper layer).  
   –  ZSPB: height of the spans measured from the lower concrete edge (lower layer).  
   –  Both in meters.  
   –  Default: 0.05 m for each.  
   –  If omitted, the tendon is placed at the slab’s middle layer.

•  FRLT (Length of straight line at supports)  
   –  For free‐layout (TYPG=PTFV), specifies the straight‐segment length on each side of a support station before curvature begins.  
   –  Unit: m.  
   –  Default: 0.30 m.

•  FRLL (Length of the transition section)  
   –  For free‐layout only, defines how long the duct transitions between upper and lower layers through the slab depth.  
   –  Unit: m.  
   –  Default: 3.00 m.

•  LC (Load case ID)  
   –  Associates the tendon to a particular load case, see record TEND for details.  
   –  Dimensionless.  
   –  Default: 0.

•  TITL (Title of the tendon)  
   –  Free text, up to 32 characters, used for annotation or identification in output.  
   –  Unit: LIT32.  
   –  No default (dash).

In practice, a minimal SLAB call for a free‐layout tendon might look like:  
 SLAB NOT 1 REFS ’TND1’ NOPS 23 TYPG PTFV ICS1 11 ICS2 12 ZSPT 0.10 ZSPB 0.10 FRLT 0.30 FRLL 3.00 …  
Followed by one or more SLBS records that specify station coordinates and elevations. This table ensures that all geometry‐defining parameters have clear descriptions, units, and sensible defaults, allowing automated parsing for RAG‐based vector storage and downstream processing.

The table shown defines the fields available in the SLBS (Slab-Bound Tendon Station) record.  This record is used to specify the position and geometry of each tendon station along a slab element.  It supports both straight and “spline” tendon layouts (the latter when the parent SLAB record uses TYPG = PTUV).  Below is a field-by-field breakdown:

1.  NOT  (Number Of Tendon)  
    – Description: Identifies which tendon (i.e. which reference axis or duct geometry) is being defined.  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: mandatory (“!”) – you must supply a value.  

2.  BIT  (Bit-Key of Constraining Point)  
    – Description: Encodes the type of station along the tendon using bit flags.  Multiple bits can be combined.  
        • 1 = support point  
        • 2 = midspan point  
        • 4 = start point  
        • 8 = end point  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: 1 (support point)  

3.  S  (Station on Plan Geometry)  
    – Description: The along-axis coordinate on the slab’s plan‐view reference axis (SLAB REFS).  Defines the horizontal location of the station.  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: S0 (start of reference axis)  

4.  ZS  (Vertical Position from Edge)  
    – Description: Elevation of the tendon within the slab cross section, measured from the nearest surface.  
        • ZS =  0.00 → placed at mid-depth  
        • ZS >  0.00 → distance from top edge  
        • ZS <  0.00 → distance from bottom edge  
      If omitted, the slab record’s ZSPT (top layer) or ZSPB (bottom layer) is used.  
    – Unit: meters  
    – Default: “*” (use slab default)  

5.  DZS  (Vertical Inclination)  
    – Description: Slope of the tendon at this station, in vertical direction.  At support and midspan points (BIT=1 or 2) the default is 0.0 to prevent the tendon from exiting the slab.  
    – Unit: none  
    – Default: “*” (zero or inherited)  

6.  DL, DR, RV, RL  (Spline-Geometry Properties)  
    These four parameters apply only when the slab’s tendon geometry type is PTUV (spline).  They define how the curve transitions between straight segments and radii:  
      • DL (Left straight length): length of the straight‐line segment preceding the curve, in the negative reference‐axis direction.  
      • DR (Right straight length): length of the straight‐line segment following the curve, in the positive reference‐axis direction.  
      • RV (Vertical radius): radius of curvature in the vertical‐plane bend.  
      • RL (Radius influence length): distance over which the radius transitions from straight to curved.  

    – Unit: meters  
    – Default: “–” (not used for straight layouts; must be supplied for spline bends)  

Remark on backward compatibility: although the SLBS record can hold additional undocumented items, always prefix each value with its item name (e.g. “DL 2.3”).  

Bit-flags example: to mark an end support, set BIT = 1 (support) + 8 (end) = 9.  

Putting it all together, a typical spline station definition might look like:  
  SLBS NOT 2 BIT 2 S 12.5 DL 2.5 DR 2.5 RV 1.2 RL 0.8  

This line defines tendon #2, at midspan (bit 2), station 12.5 m along the slab reference axis, with a 2.5 m approach straight on each side, a 1.2 m vertical bend radius and a 0.8 m transition length.

The graphical representation of the prestressing is designed for a clear assignment of the tendons and not for a complete three-dimensional representation, which is reserved for the programs WinGRAF and ANIMATOR.
 For the sake of clarity, the representations are related to a horizontal projection (x-y-plane) and to a side view/elevation transverse to the reference axis (x-z-plane). Elements, ducts and tendons are ’unrolled’ along the reference axis, which is thus always a straight line – regardless of the actual curvature.
 The following input records are available for the generation of the graphical representations:
 SIZE Sheet size and scale.
 Main command for generating plan and elevation views as well as force diagrams.
 AND Linking command to combine multiple PLOTs.
 Sets colours, line widths, fill pattern and line types, or disables plot elements.
 SCHR Sets font sizes, or disabled plot elements.

The table shown is a parameter‐reference for the TENDON module’s SIZE command, which controls sheet format, engineering scale and border settings when generating drawings.  It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and lists six parameters that you can pass to SIZE.  Below is a detailed breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG vector store:

1.  Table Structure  
    •  Columns:  
       –  Item: the keyword to be used in the SIZE command (TYPE, SC, W, H, MARG, FORM).  
       –  Description: human-readable summary of what the keyword does and, where applicable, which numeric or symbolic values it accepts.  
       –  Unit: unit of measure or literal type expected (e.g. cm, LIT4, or “—” if none).  
       –  Default: the value automatically assumed if the keyword is omitted (“*” means “module default” or “largest possible,” “–URS” is the fixed paper‐size code).

2.  Context & Related Commands  
    •  SIZE is one of the basic SOFiSTiK drawing-control commands (see “Basics: SOFISTICS: SIZE”).  
    •  The TENDON module automatically enforces FORM URS whenever TYPE ≠ –URS; URS refers to the standard A-series frames defined in the Report Browser (File → Project Options → Print → Page Frame).  
    •  When used without explicit SC, the largest engineering scale that fits the chosen format is selected.  Force diagrams always stretch to fill the paper regardless of SC.  
    •  See also: PLOT (plot‐area definitions), AND (annotation settings), COLO (color control), SCHH (hatch patterns).

3.  Parameter Details  

   •  TYPE  
      –  Definition: sets the paper format code.  
      –  Values:  
         •  Positive integer → selects a landscape A-series sheet.  
         •  Negative integer → selects the corresponding portrait sheet.  
      –  Unit: —  
      –  Default: –URS (standard URS frame).  
      –  Notes: if you supply any value other than –URS or URS, the TENDON module will override it back to FORM URS.

   •  SC  
      –  Definition: determines the drawing scale.  
      –  Values:  
         •  0 → fill the entire actual sheet size (format-filling).  
         •  * → automatically use the largest possible engineering scale that fits.  
         •  n → explicit scale of 1 : n.  
      –  Unit: —  
      –  Default: * (largest possible engineering scale, except force diagrams).

   •  W (Width)  
      –  Definition: physical sheet width or drawing area width.  
      –  Unit: cm  
      –  Default: * (calculated from TYPE if unspecified).

   •  H (Height)  
      –  Definition: physical sheet height or drawing area height.  
      –  Unit: cm  
      –  Default: * (calculated from TYPE if unspecified).

   •  MARG  
      –  Definition: toggles drawing of the sheet border.  
      –  Unit: LIT4 (literal 4-character code, e.g. ‘ON’, ‘OFF’).  
      –  Default: * (module default, usually “ON”).

   •  FORM  
      –  Definition: selects the style of the drawn border (URS frames or custom).  
      –  Unit: LIT4  
      –  Default: * (URS if TYPE ≠ URS, else module default).

4.  Example Usage  
    •  To set an A3 landscape sheet at 1 : 75 scale with URS border:  
       SIZE TYPE 3  SC 75  FORM URS  
    •  Omit W and H unless you require nonstandard dimensions.  
    •  Use PLOT, AND, COLO, SCHH for further plot‐frame, annotation, color and hatch pattern controls.

This description captures each column’s meaning, allowed values, default behaviors, inter-parameter dependencies (e.g. TYPE vs. FORM), and situates SIZE within the broader SOFiSTiK/TENDON drawing workflow.

See also: PLOT, AND, COLO, SCHH
 SIZE
 With the SIZE command, sheet size and scale can be set. The command is one of the basic functions and was slightly modified for the TENDON module.
 The documentation for SIZE can be found in the manual ’Basics’: SOFISTICS: SIZE.
 SC By default the largest possible engineering scale is chosen. Exception: Force diagrams are always drawn to fill the format.
 FORM Only FORM URS is supported. In case TYPE is not -URS or URS, FORM URS has to be set (or will be set automatically by TENDON). Note: (ZTV) frames can be set in the Report Browser: File → Project Options → Print → Page Frame.

This table documents the PLOT record’s parameters for controlling plan views, elevation views and force diagrams of ducts and tendons in SOFiSTiK.  It is intended for ingestion into a RAG-style vector store, so each field is broken out with its semantic role, allowed values, units and defaults.

1. RECORD CONTEXT  
   • PLOT – top-level drawing record for duct geometries (GEOE/GEOP), tendons (TNDE/TNDP) and force diagrams (FACT).  
   • See also:  
     – SOFISTIK: SIZE  (global drawing scale and text size)  
     – AND/COLO/SCHH  (line styles, colors, hatch patterns)

2. FIELD DESCRIPTIONS

1) SHOW  
   • Role: Selects which type of graphic to produce.  
   • Allowed values (LIT4):  
     – “TNDE” = tendon in elevation view  
     – “T NDP” = tendon in plan view  
     – “GEOE” = duct in elevation view  
     – “GEOP” = duct in plan view  
     – “FACT” = force‐diagram of internal forces  
   • Default: TNDE  
   • Notes: Mutually exclusive; determines the semantics of the ID field that follows.

2) NO  
   • Role: Identifier of the entity to draw, corresponding to the SHOW setting.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – “ALL” or 0 to draw all items in the database  
     – For SHOW=TNDE/TNDP/FACT: use tendon ID “NOT”  
     – For SHOW=GEOE/GEOP: use duct geometry ID “NOG”  
   • Type: integer or literal up to 4 chars  
   • Default: ALL

3) FACH  
   • Role: “Superelevation factor” – vertical exaggeration or compression for plot.  
   • Unit: dimensionless real  
   • Behavior:  
     – < 10.0 → shifts the force zero line upward (compressed display)  
     – > 10.0 → shifts the zero line downward (stretched display)  
   • Default: 10.0  
   • Only applies when SHOW=FACT (force diagram).  In plan/elevation, it has no effect.

4) TYPG  
   • Role: Type of curve(s) to include in the drawing.  
   • Allowed values (LIT4):  
     – “DUCT” → draw only the duct geometry  
     – “TEND” → draw only the tendon path  
     – “DUTE” → draw both duct and tendon curves  
     – “ALL” → same as DUTE plus reference axes (gravity and alignment)  
   • Default: ALL  
   • Notes: Only meaningful for plan/elevation views (SHOW=GEOP/GEOE/TNDP/TNDE).  Ignored when SHOW=FACT.

5) FROM / TO  
   • Role: Longitudinal limits of the plot in stationing (curve parameter).  
   • Unit: same coordinate units as curve definition (meters by default).  
   • Default: ‘*’ (automatic): limits are taken from the min/max of the selected duct or tendon.  
   • Notes: Available only for plan and elevation views; no effect on force diagrams.

6) PCS  
   • Role: Tendon overview toggle: draws the domain (definition range) of all tendons.  
   • Allowed values: integer  
     – 0 → do not show the tendon range  
     – ≠0 → show the definition domains as a bounding box or line for all tendons  
   • Default: 0  
   • Notes: Only applies to plan/elevation (SHOW=GEOP/GEOE/TNDP/TNDE).  Shows the extents, not the curve itself.

3. USAGE EXAMPLES  
– Minimum output (all tendon elevation + force diagram):  
  PLOT GEOE  
  PLOT FACT  

– Duct + tendon overview only:  
  PLOT GEOE NO 102 FACH 15.0 TYPG DUCT PCS 1

4. RELATIONSHIPS  
• SHOW determines which IDs (NO) and settings (TYPG, PCS, FACH) are valid.  
• FROM/TO always bound the view but default to the full curve range.  
• FACH only modulates vertical scaling in force diagrams.  
• TYPG permits isolating or combining geometry and tendon curves for clarity.

See also: SIZE, AND, COLO, SCHH
 PLOT

The table under analysis defines a series of fourteen “F-items” (F1 through F14), each of which corresponds to a distinct graphic element in a plot or engineering diagram.  It assigns to each element a default four-digit styling code (“Default”) that follows the COLO record convention:

  •  Digit 1 (thousands place): colour index (1=black, 2=red, 3=green, 4=blue, 5=yellow, 6=brown, 7=grey, 8=light blue, 9=orange)  
  •  Digit 2 (hundreds place): width factor (when non‐zero, width in tenths—for example “2” → 2.0, “25”→2.5)  
  •  Digits 3–4 (tens + ones): stroke type for lines or fill pattern for areas  
       – Lines: 1=solid, 2=dashed, 3=dotted, 4=dash-dotted, 5=narrow dashed, 6=narrow dotted  
       – Fills: 1=dotted, 2=crossed, 3=blank, 4=filled  

A code of zero in any position suppresses that aspect.

ROW-BY-ROW SUMMARY  
1. F1 “Legend” – Default 1101  
   •  Colour=1 (black), width=1.0, stroke/fill type=01 (solid line for legends).  

2. F2 “Tendon” – Default 2251  
   •  Colour=2 (red), width=2.5, stroke type=1 (solid).  Red, thick solid line used to represent prestressing tendons.  

3. F3 “Force in force diagram” – Default 2251  
   •  Same styling as tendons: red, width 2.5, solid.  Ensures forces in the diagram stand out in bold red.  

4. F4 “Evaluation points in the force diagram” – Default 7101

5. F5 “Contour of elements” – Default 1101  
   •  Black solid lines for outlining finite‐element mesh or structural elements.  

6. F6 “Axis of gravity” – Default 8204  
   •  Colour=8 (light blue), width=2.0, stroke type=4 (dash-dotted).  A distinctive dash-dotted light-blue line for the gravity axis.  

7. F7 “Indicated prestressing sequence” – Default 1106  
   •  Colour=1 (black), width=1.0, stroke type=6 (narrow dotted).  

8. F8 “Force levels” – Default 1101  
   •  Black solid lines to indicate force magnitudes or level lines.  

9. F9 “Reference axis” – Default 4102  
   •  Colour=4 (blue), width=1.0, stroke type=2 (dashed).  Blue dashed reference axis.  

10. F10 “Characteristic points in the force diagram” – Default 8101  
    •  Colour=8 (light blue), width=1.0, stroke type=1 (solid).  

11. F11 “Fill pattern of beam elements” – Default 5001  
    •  Colour=5 (yellow), fill pattern=1 (dotted).  Yellow-dotted fill for beam cross-sections or areas.  

12. F12 “Fill pattern of quad elements” – Default 9001  
    •  Colour=9 (orange), fill=1 (dotted).  Orange-dotted fill for quadrilateral finite elements.  

13. F13 “Contour of the duct” – Default 1101  
    •  Black solid line for duct outlines.  

14. F14 “Mid axis of the duct” – Default 8206  
    •  Colour=8 (light blue), width=2.0, stroke type=6 (narrow dotted).  

By encoding these defaults, any plotting routine reading the COLO record can automatically render each feature with consistent colour, line thickness, and patterning.

The table on SCHH items provides a concise mapping between adjustable caption categories in a plotting context and their corresponding default font‐size multipliers. It is intended for use with a plotting or graphic module (see also PLOT, AND, COLO) that supports a SCHH control record enabling the user to scale or suppress individual text captions. Each row in the table represents one caption category, identified by an “H” code from H1 through H8. The four columns are:

 1. Item  
    – A code (H1–H8) that identifies a specific caption or label group in the graphic output.  
 2. Description  
    – A brief human‐readable explanation of what the code controls. For instance, H1 controls the legend text, while H4 sets the size for station numbers and force‐factor annotations.  
 3. Unit  
    – Not applicable in this context (all entries are shown as “—”); because SCHH deals strictly with font‐size scaling factors relative to a default, there is no physical unit.  
 4. Default  
    – The standard multiplier applied to the default font size. All categories default to 1.0, meaning that, unless overridden, captions appear at the base font size. Specifying a value greater than 1.0 enlarges that caption group proportionally; setting it to 0.0 suppresses the captions entirely.

Detailed breakdown of each caption code:

 H1 Legend  
   Controls the font size used for the plot legend.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H2 Arc length, distances (u,v) and inclinations  
   Governs the text size for geometric annotations—arc lengths, vector distances in the u‐v plane, and angle or inclination markers.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H3 Forces and stresses  
   Applies to numerical or symbolic labels that indicate force magnitudes or stress values on elements.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H4 Stations and force factors  
   Sets the lettering size for station numbers (e.g., positions along a beam or profile) and any associated force‐factor indicators.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H5 Element ids  
   Affects the size of element identification labels (element numbers or names).  
   Default: 1.0  

 H6 Node ids  
   Adjusts the font for node identifiers—points in a mesh or framework.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H7 Tendon and duct labels  
   Controls the appearance of labels attached to tendons, ducts, or similar embedded lines/traces.  
   Default: 1.0  

 H8 Force levels  
   Manages text showing discrete force‐level lines or contour labels (e.g., in stress‐contour plots).  
   Default: 1.0  

Usage example: to double the legend’s font size you would issue  
  SCHH H1 2.0  
and to hide the element IDs completely you would set  
  SCHH H5 0.0  

By capturing these eight categories, the SCHH record lets users fine‐tune the readability and visual hierarchy of complex engineering and geometric plots without affecting global font‐size settings.

In this chapter, the calculation of the immediate force losses of module TENDON is to be illustrated with a simple example and the correctness is to be confirmed with hand calculations. The notation essentially follows [2].

The figure shows a single‐span, simply supported concrete beam of total span L = 20 m that is prestressed by a single, concentric circular tendon (drawn in red) running the full length of the beam. Above the beam a circle of radius R = 20 m is sketched in outline: its center lies on the vertical mid‐span axis, at a distance z₁ = 10·√3 m above the top fiber of the beam. Two radii drawn from that center meet the top surface of the beam at an opening angle ϕ = 60° (split symmetrically into 30° on each side of the vertical). These radial lines mark the exact points where the tendon leaves the top chord of the concrete section to begin its circular profile.  

Inside the shaded grey region (the beam’s cross-section), the tendon is shown as a smooth red arc subtending the same 60° central angle. At mid‐span the tendon reaches its lowest point, which lies a vertical distance z₂ = R – z₁ = 20 m – 10·√3 m below the top of the beam (numerically about 2.68 m). Horizontally, the half‐span “offset” from mid‐span to the point where the tendon meets the beam boundary is x = R·sin(30°) = 10 m, forming a right angle with the mid‐span vertical axis.  

Beneath the beam ends, simple triangular supports indicate pinned‐end boundary conditions. The tendon profile is perfectly symmetric about mid‐span, reflecting the fact that eccentricity of the duct inside the concrete was deactivated. All relevant prestressing parameters appear in the accompanying text:
• Radius of curvature R = 20 m and opening angle ϕ = 60° (π/3 rad)  
• Eccentricity e = 0  
• Initial jack load P₀ = 1 000 kN (σ₀ = 1 000 N/mm²) with steel area Aₚ = 1 000 mm²  
• Steel Young’s modulus Eₚ = 205·10³ N/mm²  
• Slip at anchorage Δs = 4 mm  
• Friction coefficient μ = 0.61  
• Wobble coefficient β = 0.005 rad/m  

Together, the geometric sketch and these parameters fully define the tendon’s circular layout, the depth variation within the beam section, and the factors that will influence force‐transition losses during prestress transfer.

Given is the following simple beam, prestressed with a circular tendon.
 The following parameters have an influence on the force transition loss (see Teddy input 4.5):
 • Duct tube and tendon are circular with a radius of R = 20m, and an opening angle ϕ = 60◦ = π 3 rd. An eccentricity of the tendon inside the duct is deactivated.
 • The jacking force (stress) is chosen with P0 = 1000kN (or σ0 = 1000N/mm2). The prestressing steel area is thus 1000mm2 = 1 · 10−3 m2.
 • The selected prestressing steel has a Young’s modulus of EP = 205 · 103 N/mm2 = 205 · 106 kN/m2.
 • The slip shall be Δs = 4mm.
 • The friction coefficient is set to be μ = 0.61.
 • The wobble factor is β = 0.005rd/m (Please refer to section 4.4).

The figure is a two‐dimensional plot of axial force P (vertical axis) versus arc length x along a circular tendon (horizontal axis). It illustrates how “slip” between the tendon and its surrounding sheath corresponds to the area between two force curves: the jacking (tensioning) curve P(x) and the slip (release) curve P′(x). Below is a breakdown of all key graphic elements, annotations and their mathematical significance:

1. Coordinate Axes  
   • Vertical axis (ordinate) labeled “P”. At the very top, a horizontal tick and label “P₀” denote the maximum jacking force applied at the anchor before any slip. Below that, a second horizontal tick marks “P′₀”, the reduced anchor force after slip has been applied.  
   • Horizontal axis (abscissa) represents the arc length coordinate x, measured from the fixed jacking anchor at x = 0 outward along the tendon. A single tick on this axis is labeled “lₛₗ”, the so‐called “influence length” over which slip occurs.

2. The Jacking (Tensioning) Curve P(x)  
   • Depicted as a grey dotted line starting at P(0) = P₀ on the vertical axis and curving downward toward the right.  • Its analytic form is given by  
     P(x) = P₀ ⋅ e^(–μ [Σθ(x) + β x])  
     which captures the exponential decay of force along the tendon due to friction (coefficient μ), cumulative angular displacement Σθ(x), and straight‐length contribution βx.

3. The Slip (Release) Curve P′(x)  
   • Drawn as a continuous red line in two segments:  
     – From x = 0 to x = lₛₗ the red curve actually rises from P′₀ at x = 0 up to the intersection point at x = lₛₗ.  – Beyond x = lₛₗ the red curve bends smoothly downward, following the same exponential form as the dotted jacking curve but offset, reflecting how the force reduces as slip propagates.  
   • Its functional form is noted alongside the rising segment:  
     P′(x) = P′₀ ⋅ e^(+μ [Σθ(x) + β x])  
     and alongside the falling segment (coinciding with the dotted grey formula for P(x) except driven from the original P₀ anchor).

4. The Intersection Point (x = lₛₗ)  
   • A vertical dashed blue line marks x = lₛₗ, the “slip influence length.”  • At this coordinate the two curves meet: P(lₛₗ) = P′(lₛₗ).  • That equality ensures the force carried by the tendon under tensioning equals the force after slip release at exactly that point.

The Geometry Tendon: 201 table provides a point‐by‐point discretization of a curved tendon path, generated by cubic spline interpolation, and reports key geometric quantities—coordinates, inclinations, local arc lengths, curvature radii, accumulated angular rotations and eccentricities—at equally spaced stations along a reference axis from 0 m to 20 m. A brief walk-through of its structure and contents follows:

1. Stationing and Element ID  
   • Station [–]: the longitudinal coordinate along the reference axis, in meters, sampled at 0, 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 m.  
   • Element Id: an index (1–5) identifying each beam element connecting consecutive stations.  
   • Element Type: all entries are “Beam,” indicating beam‐element segments in the finite‐element model.

2. Coordinates (u, v)  
   • u [m], v [m]: local coordinates of the tendon curve referred to the reference axis.  
   • The tendon rises from (0.000, 0.000) at station 0 to a maximum offset of (0.000, 2.579) at station 8 m and descends symmetrically back to (0.000, 0.000) at station 20 m, tracing a circular arc.

3. Inclination (du/dx, dv/dx)  
   • Slopes of u and v with respect to the reference axis, dimensionless.  
   • du/dx remains zero throughout (pure vertical bending), while dv/dx increases to +0.3145 at 4 m, then decreases symmetrically to –0.3145 at 16 m.

4. Arc Length and Radius  
   • Arc len [m]: cumulative length of the interpolated tendon curve measured from station 0. It grows from 0.000 m up to 20.944 m at station 20.  
   • Radius [m]: local radius of curvature. All tabulated values are 20.00 m, reflecting an intended circular arc; however, spline interpolation yields a slight deviation in minimum radius (19.987 m at station 10.164 m).

5. Angle and Eccentricity  
   • Angle [–]: accumulated bending angle in radians at each station, starting from 0 rad at station 0 to 1.047 rad (≈60°) at station 20.  
   • Ecc [mm]: lateral eccentricity of the tendon relative to the duct curve; all entries are zero, implying perfect centering.

6. Summary Metrics (footnotes)  
   • Reference-axis total arc length: 20.000 m  
   • Tendon-curve total arc length: 20.944 m  
   • Sum of angular change: 1.047 rad (≈60°)  
   • Minimum radius of curvature: 19.987 m (at station 10.164 m)

Below is a structured, detailed description of the “Force Factors Tendon: 201” table. This description is suitable for use in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) vector store, and it contains all key metadata, units, definitions and contextual notes.  

1. Table Identity  
   • Title: Force Factors Tendon: 201  
   • Purpose: Reports dimensionless force‐reduction (or amplification) factors along the length of a prestressed tendon during successive tensioning and slip steps. Provides both relative factors (per reference force) and absolute jack forces/elongations.  

2. Context & Reference  
   • The factors in the table are expressed with respect to a “reference force” (e.g. 1000 kN in this example).  
   • The reference force is defined in record SYSP item ZV or via the “Prestressing Systems” dialogue in the graphical workflow.  
   • Command PLOT FACT will print the force diagram in the project report.  
   • Footnotes:  
     1. Forces acting on a single tendon in each stressing/release step at the jack (TEND INTEN=1).  
     2. Elongation per step: positive when re-stressed, negative when released/slip.  

3. Column Definitions  
   1. Station [–]  
      – Chainage position along the tendon (0 = anchorage start, increasing toward free end).  
   2. Arc len [m]  
      – Cumulative curved length of tendon from station 0.  
   3. Left side factors (per prestress step)  
      – Stres (Stressing factor)  
      – Relea (Releasing factor)  
      – Restr (Restressing factor)  
      – Slip (Slip factor)  
      – LoadA (Load application factor for PDAT or TEND EFRO/ETO commands)  
   4. Right side factors (mirror of Left)  
      – Stres, Restr, Slip, LoadA  
   5. active  
      – Net active force factor after the listed step (dimensionless).  

4. Rows & Data Patterns  
   • Six discrete stations are sampled every 4 m of arc length:  
     – Station 0.000 m (Arc len 0.000 m)  
     – Station 4.000 m (4.378 m)  
     – Station 8.000 m (8.469 m)  
     – Station 12.000 m (12.475 m)  
     – Station 16.000 m (16.566 m)  
     – Station 20.000 m (20.944 m)  
   • Only the “Left – Stressing” and “Left – Slip” columns are populated for prestress sequence 1; columns under sequence 2 and all right-side columns remain blank in this excerpt.  
   • Stressing factors decrease progressively from 1.00 at station 0 to 0.50 at station 20.  
   • Slip factors likewise track from 0.70 down to 0.50.  
   • The “active” factor (effective force factor) follows the combination of stressing and slip, ranging from 0.698 at station 0 to 0.501 at station 20.  

5. Summary of Key Values (Bottom Section)  
   – Jack force single [kN]: 1000.0 kN (reference jack force)  
   – Slip-related jack force [kN]: 698.1 kN (1000 kN × 0.698 at station 0)

   – Remark: Elongations shown do NOT include elastic shortening within concrete or steel.
